item.title: The Hit Song ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Hits a Nerve: Is Texas the South?
item.description:
On a recent Saturday night at Ego’s, a popular Austin karaoke bar, the room went quiet as two young women stepped onto the stage.

The lyrics to Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” flashed across the screen in changing colors, but few in the crowd were looking. They knew the words by heart.

At the song’s chorus, the room exploded into song.

“As soon as that riff comes in, everybody loses their minds,” said Harrison Anderson, a musician and D.J. who hosts Thursday night karaoke at Hole in the Wall, another Austin venue.

Days earlier, the Pinnacle, a Nashville live music venue, was packed with some of country music’s biggest behind-the-scenes figures. They erupted into applause for Ms. Langley, who had taken home yet another music award, while someone performed a cover of “Choosin’ Texas.” Ms. Langley shared her gratitude for the award remotely.

Nashville is singing along to a song about choosing Texas. Nobody seems to mind.

“Choosin’ Texas” has spent 20 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, claiming the longest run ever atop the chart for a non-holiday song.

Ms. Langley, who is notably not from Texas — though a co-writer, Miranda Lambert, is — has tapped into the mythology of the Lone Star State, as well as an age-old musical rivalry with Tennessee.

The song arrives at a moment when the calling cards of Southern culture — its music and fashion, even its college football traditions — have spread far beyond the region. Among those cultural exports, the image of Texas has emerged at the forefront.

“It’s like this perfect storm with this song,” said Leslie Fram, a former Country Music Television executive who now works with musicians and artists in Nashville. She added, “The audience wants authenticity.”

There’s just one wrinkle: Texas has spent more than a century insisting that it isn’t really Southern.

“Southerners can be very strict about who is Southern, but grudgingly include Texas because almost everything about them is Southern,” said Beverly Keel, a former music journalist and publicist who now oversees the media and entertainment college at Middle Tennessee State University. And, she added, “Texas and Tennessee, from my perspective, have always been friendly rivals.”

Texas has long straddled South and West, said Glen Sample Ely, a Texas historian and author of “Where the West Begins: Debating Texas Identity.” East Texas was shaped by slavery and the cotton economy, while farther west, the arid landscape and demands of frontier defense more closely resembled the American West.

But after the Civil War and Reconstruction, Texas increasingly emphasized its Western identity, distancing itself from Confederate defeat and elevating the Alamo and the frontier as foundational myths. (It was, at one point, its own country, a distinction some Texans still embrace.)

“The key to its identity is branding,” Mr. Ely said.

Today, the Texas brand has traveled far beyond state lines, becoming shorthand abroad for country music and American culture. In Tokyo, a well-known bar and restaurant goes by the name Little Texas.

“You’re kind of talking about the Confederacy versus cowboys, and you can see which one would travel well versus the other,” said Jamal Khadar, writer and host of the British radio show “Reimagining Country.”

Texas has its own music charts and its own music scene, often showcasing the “red dirt” genre that originated in Oklahoma. But the business of country music has always run through Nashville, even as the cowboys and open roads came from Texas.

That has meant generations of the state’s biggest stars — from Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings to Miranda Lambert and Kacey Musgraves — have looked to Nashville to expand their careers. But it also often meant coming home to Texas, whether to record or build a business.

“Nashville is the producer but Texas is the product,” Mr. Khadar said.

In Nashville, it was clear Ms. Langley, a rising star, had a bona fide country hit on her hands with “Choosin’ Texas.” (The song is also co-written with Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor, both Nashville-based songwriters.)

It invoked familiar symbols from both states — Memphis blues, Jack Daniel’s whiskey, Interstate 40 drives and two-stepping — alongside a simple, contagious melody and a familiar story of heartbreak.

The surprise for some, however, came when it went beyond — with its traditional twangy lamentations, steel guitar and country music trappings.

“It was having a kernel of authenticity with a native Texan in there in the writing room invoking that mythology and grandeur and culture of Texas, in order to tell a story,” said Dwayne O’Brien, a founding member of the band Little Texas who teaches at Belmont University in Nashville. And, he added, “country music is now pitching an even bigger tent than it ever has before.”

That sense of Texas exceptionalism may also help explain the song’s popularity. In the Lone Star State, it has become something of a regional rallying cry. In early August, Matthew McConaughey, another beloved Texas export, performed a bluegrass-style cover of the song on “The Tonight Show.” Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas put it atop his end-of-summer playlist.

“One of the oldest tricks in the book in country songwriting is to mention different states and cities,” said Alan Richard, the author of the Southern American music blog “Soul Country.” “For marketing purposes, it’s always good to mention Texas or California or some humongous place.”

He added, “People find themselves in songs like that.”

What that means for the song’s place in country music’s history is harder to settle.

“I can’t tell you the last time I can think of a very traditional country song also going No. 1 pop,” said Paul Kingsbury, the senior director of editorial research at the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum.

“We’ll have to mention it — it’s so big,” he added. “But exactly how we’re going to treat it? No, we don’t know right now.”

Emily asked me one afternoon over Slack: "Is there something to do about Tennessee and Texas battling it out for Southern cultural supremacy?” She’d been thinking about the question in the context of Ella Langley’s surprise hit.“Well, as you’re probably already aware, most people don’t even consider Texas the South,” I wrote back.“Count me as one of those people,” she replied. “Respectfully!”And so began our inquiry into the “friendly rivalry” between Texas and Tennessee.

item.title: Can a ‘Prairie Populist’ Democrat Win a Senate Seat in Trump’s Iowa?
item.description:
Josh Turek pushed past the Ring-a-Duck and the Tilt-a-Whirl before rolling up to the Iowa State Fair staple called Hot Shot.

“Big Game,” a sign said. “Big Prizes.”

“You just gotta make two?” he asked.

Sitting in his wheelchair with spoked wheels and an aluminum, titanium and carbon fiber frame, Mr. Turek spun a basketball in his hands. A two-time Paralympic gold medalist, he dribbled hard twice, then twice more.

On the busy, noisy midway, reporters, photographers and passers-by stopped and watched.

Mr. Turek, 47, had attracted a crowd not simply on account of athletic renown. He is the rare Democrat seen as having a plausible path to winning a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, where he faces Ashley Hinson, a three-term Republican congresswoman and former local news anchor, in a high-stakes race with the potential to help his party win back control of the upper chamber.

At first glance, he is an unlikely key to his party’s hopes. The first time he cast a ballot for president, he was a registered Republican and voted for George W. Bush. In a moment marked by the rise of democratic socialists, he identifies as a “common-sense prairie populist.” And in this era of extreme polarization, he touts the times he’s voted with Republicans. He says he will work with anybody — including President Trump.

He sticks out, too, on the short list of Democrats’ top Senate hopefuls. Compared to Roy Cooper of North Carolina, Sherrod Brown of Ohio or Mary Peltola of Alaska, he had no record of statewide electoral success until he won his primary in June. Relative to charismatic candidates like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, James Talarico of Texas or Jon Ossoff of Georgia, Mr. Turek lacks a certain stage presence and oratorical buzz.

But in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in 18 years and that Mr. Trump won in 2024 by more than 13 points, polls and independent analysts suggest Mr. Turek has a chance.

And he recently earned his party’s ultimate imprimatur: Former President Barack Obama backed him in a video in which he called Mr. Turek “somebody who knows how to win.”

Ms. Hinson is trying to paint Mr. Turek as more liberal than he lets on and as a lawmaker who’s missed too many votes. “My opponent is an absentee legislator,” she said in an interview. But her allies acknowledge that targeting Mr. Turek is uncommonly complicated.

Voters and politicians alike assign to Mr. Turek traits like resilience and persistence — a sense, judging from conversations around the state, that’s based less on what he says and more on what they see.

“Determination,” said Tom Harkin, Iowa’s last Democratic senator. “An ethic of not letting anything hold you back.”

“Toughness,” Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona said. “What he’s had to overcome.”

“There is a stigma associated with individuals with disabilities that maybe we’re not quite as capable as the average individual,” Mr. Turek said in an interview. “I think I’m always battling that stigma.”

But, he added, “there is a benefit. That put some serious ambition in me — like, look, I’m going to prove to you what I can do and what I can accomplish.”

At Hot Shot, Mr. Turek looked up and took aim. His first ball missed, off the front of the rim and too far to the left. So did his second, off the front, too far to the right. He missed another, and then another.

“I’m doing it again,” he said.

Mr. Turek was born in Council Bluffs, on Iowa’s western edge, to parents coping with grief. Their first child, Tasha, had drowned as a toddler in a pool.

Joshua Turek was their third.

He came out breech, and his father saw in the eyes of the doctor that something was wrong. At the bottom of the baby’s back was a fluid-filled bulge of balled-up nerves — spina bifida, the family later learned, presumably caused by his father’s exposure during his service in Vietnam to the jungle-killing poison known as Agent Orange. The next day, Josh had the first of more than 20 surgeries.

His parents had three more children, and the family lived on not much money. His father was a recruiter for a local technical school, and his mother was a county case worker for the mentally disabled. They shopped at Goodwill. The kids shared clothes and ate free lunch at school and tuna noodle casserole and gravy on toast at home. They went to family nights at the Royal Fork Buffet when anybody under 12 ate for 10 cents times their age. They never talked about their father’s necklace — a locket with a picture of their older sister who had died.

The Tureks’ oldest boy had surgery after surgery on his clubfoot, his faulty hips and his stunted spine. He didn’t crawl until he was 3. He didn’t walk until he was 5. He lugged his legs with a herky-jerky gait until he started using a wheelchair at 10. He was bullied so badly that he moved to Missouri for middle school, living with his great aunt and attending the Christian school where she taught. Back in Council Bluffs for high school, he joined the student council, the student newspaper and the Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps. He had a graduation party at his house, and not one classmate came.

This past spring, at the YMCA in Des Moines, Mr. Turek slid out of his chair and onto a mat on the floor.

“The very first thing that my father sees is the mass of nerves on the base of my back,” he said. “I always thought that for someone like him, he would have stopped and said, ‘Oh my goodness, I’ve lost my firstborn, now we’ve had a child with disabilities, I’m not going to continue on.’”

Dressed in a white United States Paralympic Team T-shirt and navy Nike pants and shoes, Mr. Turek stretched and winced.

“But they kept going,” he said.

Mr. Turek’s younger brother and youngest sister were tall and good at basketball — good enough eventually to play in college and professionally in Europe. As kids, his siblings honed their shots on the hoop at their house. From his chair or trying to stand, he did, too.

He attended a wheelchair sports camp when he was 12 and played for the Nebraska Red Dawgs wheelchair basketball team in Omaha as a teen. He kept getting better. He wanted, he told the local newspaper, The Daily Nonpareil, to be the “wheelchair champion of the world.”

At Southwest Minnesota State University, he was a three-time team captain and a four-time National Wheelchair Basketball Association All-American. He scored more than 4,000 points.

After college, he played for a professional team in Italy. He played in the Paralympics in Athens in 2004, when the U.S. finished seventh.

In 2005, he moved to Spain to play for a team near Madrid. But when he tried out for Team USA, he got cut.

He got cut in 2006.

He got cut in 2007 and 2008.

He got cut in 2009 and 2010.

He was always a top-shelf scorer, according to teammates, but had to become a better defender. In Council Bluffs between seasons in Spain, he lifted weights at the Y and pressed through laps around Lake Manawa.

He played in the Paralympics in London in 2012, scoring 15 points to help the U.S. beat Britain to win the bronze medal. He played in Rio de Janeiro in 2016, scoring four points against Turkey in the semifinals to help the U.S. win the gold. And he played in Tokyo in 2021, when the U.S. won the gold again.

“I was sad with how I played, particularly in the last two games,” he told The Nonpareil. “Maybe there’s something poetic about the great scorer in his last game scoring zero points,” he said, “totally satisfied because the ultimate goal was to win a gold medal for your country.”

Even as he was creating a life as an athlete, he was steadily thinking about what might come next, imagining a career in politics. In 2008, he was spotted by a reporter from the conservative National Review changing his voter registration so he could pick Mr. Obama in the caucuses. His time overseas, Mr. Turek told him, had upped his interest in government at home.

“After living in Europe,” he said, “I think it’s embarrassing that 40 million Americans don’t have health coverage.”

And after Tokyo, he was ready. He told The Nonpareil: “I don’t want basketball to be the be-all, end-all of my story.”

He tugged his wheelchair up porches and stoops.

Married to a woman from the Dominican Republic he had met in Spain, working at a wheelchair company in Omaha and driving his hand-controlled Dodge Charger around his hilly hometown, Mr. Turek decided to run for a State House seat in 2022. He went from house to house to champion more equitable health care, higher wages for workers and more funding for public schools.

“He’s had to drag himself up some stairs,” said Lisa Lima, the chair of the Democratic Party of Pottawattamie County. “They can’t just say, ‘Oh, come back another day.’”

“Always, the first question is, ‘How in the world did you get up here?’” Mr. Turek said. “And I say, ‘I dragged my wheelchair up here. That’s how important your vote is.’”

His first race, he won by six votes.

Two years later, he was re-elected by nearly 600.

In his two terms at the capitol in Des Moines, Mr. Turek was one of the more bipartisan legislators and was lauded for being one of the most effective. He voted against school vouchers and limits on books in school libraries about L.G.B.T.Q. topics. He was also one of just seven Democrats to vote with Republicans on a bill calling for longer prison sentences for serial serious offenders. And he was one of only three Democrats to vote with Republicans to attempt to make illegal immigration a state crime and to require state law enforcement to make arrests.

In this year’s Senate race, Mr. Turek won the support of several high-profile Democrats during the primary, including Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois; Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary; and Mr. Harkin, the architect of the Americans with Disabilities Act. He was the all but designated preference of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — and the beneficiary of $10 million of outside spending. It helped him trounce his closest primary opponent.

Since then, he has hand-pedaled 59 miles in a cross-Iowa bicycle ride, downed Busch Light while hobnobbing with fans at the Iowa Corn 350 stock car race and marked his final visit in a tour of all of Iowa’s 99 counties with a cheesy quip. “We intentionally had the 99th county be Worth County so we could say that this trip was worth it,” he said at Worth Brewing. The few dozen people by the bar obliged with laughs and applause.

A few hours later, at the Iowa Democratic Wing Ding Dinner in Clear Lake, he sat at the base of a ramp built for him.

The short video that had announced Mr. Obama’s support played on big screens. The former president and the potential senator dueled in a state-specific version of the basketball game of H-O-R-S-E — in which two players try to match shots. “Not only did I get whooped,” Mr. Obama said to the camera after losing in I-O-W-A, “but you’ve got here a man of character.”

Some 750 people stood and cheered. Mr. Turek pushed toward the center of the stage.

Back at the state fair, in the Agriculture Building across from the Pork Tent, Mr. Turek waited in the line to see the Butter Cow. He moved past seventh-place tomatoes, fourth-place corn and second-place squash.

A staffer offered him signature snacks. Peanut butter and jelly corn dogs. Deep-fried Oreos. Pickle pizza. He didn’t think twice.

He went with the hot beef sundae.

“This is very similar to what we’d eat as kids,” he said. “My mom would make as much as she could with potatoes and beef or rice or noodles.”

Into the Styrofoam bowl filled with mashed potatoes, roast beef and gravy, shredded cheese and a cherry tomato on top, Mr. Turek plunged his plastic spork.

At the fair’s semifamous “soapbox,” on a dais adorned with bales of hay, Mr. Turek made his pitch: Everything costs too much — gas, groceries and more — and Ms. Hinson isn’t helping, he said. She voted for Mr. Trump’s tariffs, for his war in Iran, for his “One Big Beautiful Bill” that made it harder for some Iowans to have health care, he said. He said he was “very proud” to have “voted with Republicans over 700 times” in the State House. He brings to politics, he said, lessons learned while winning medals. “It’s not about the back of the jersey. It’s about the front,” he said. “USA.”

Chip Albright, a musician from Des Moines, capped the candidate’s speech with a song, “If It’s Turek, That’s Terrific!” — a ditty as corny as it was catchy. “Tough times need good guys who overcome obstacles,” Mr. Albright sang. “Winners never quit.”

Mr. Turek’s bipartisan bent, his hokey jokes, his less than electrifying oratory — it all makes him distinct from other, edgier Democratic candidates of 2026.

“He’s boring,” said Amanda Litman, the president of Run for Something, a progressive group that recruits young candidates, who backed one of Mr. Turek’s opponents in the primary.

“The idea of him is better than the reality of him,” she said. And yet that might not be disqualifying, she added. “Actually, the idea of him might be enough.”

For any Democrat, Iowa is an uphill battle. Mr. Turek is trailing Ms. Hinson in fund-raising, and polls, too, suggest he is behind — but not by much. Some elections analysts rate the race as leaning Republican; last month, though, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report reassessed it as a tossup.

Out on the midway, he linked up with Mr. Kelly, the senator from Arizona — here to stump for Mr. Turek, and to seed some ambitions of his own.

Mr. Kelly asked Mr. Turek about playing basketball with Mr. Obama.

It was stressful, he said. “He runs out, like, 12 straight shots — bang, bang, bang,” said Mr. Turek, wheeling past the Tornado, the Sizzler and a stall selling strawberry daiquiris.

“And I was, like, ‘I’m playing the president of the United States, one of my political heroes.’ I’m, like, ‘I’m gonna choke under the lights here. I’m never gonna hear the end of this from Paralympians.’”

At Hot Shot, surrounded by the reporters, photographers and passers-by, Mr. Turek held his hand high as his fifth shot flew through the air — the ball bouncing off the front rim, off the back rim, and finally in. He made his sixth try, too. For his prize, he picked a plush steer.

“Once I’m warm,” he said, “I’m good.”

Georgia Gee contributed research. Bayliss Wagner contributed reporting from Des Moines.

item.title: North Carolina Mails First Ballots of Fall, as Trump Tries to Restrict Them
item.description:
North Carolina began sending mail ballots to voters early on Friday, the first state to forge ahead with its standard vote-by-mail program as the Trump administration escalates its efforts to restrict the practice.

State election officials said they would send their first batch of absentee ballots just after midnight on Friday to the more than 46,000 voters who have requested them. More ballots will go out as more requests come in.

The mailing of ballots could complicate the Trump administration’s effort to impose new restrictions on voting by mail, which it claims without evidence is intended to root out tens of thousands of noncitizens who are illegally registered to vote.

The administration is trying to apply a rule that calls for states to hand over voter data, and requires a particular ballot envelope design that would allow the U.S. Postal Service to scan a bar code as part of a voter verification process. The rule also threatens to withhold mail delivery of ballots in states that don’t comply.

However, with the fall election just nine weeks away and administrators already starting to send out mail ballots, a federal judge’s temporary block of the rule has put the government in a race against the clock. Nineteen other states are set to mail ballots to voters by Sept. 19.

Election officials in many of those states, including North Carolina, have said it wasn’t likely they could carry out the new rule if the courts decided to allow it to take effect.

“It is far too late in the election cycle to introduce such dramatic changes,” said Marc Brunton, North Carolina’s deputy attorney general, in a filing last week in the case, in which about two dozen states sued the postal service in federal court in Massachusetts to block the rule. The states argue that the rule violates the Constitution, which gives states and Congress, not the executive branch, the power to run elections.

A top election official in Wisconsin said in court filings this week that it would be “virtually impossible” for the state to comply with the new requirements. In Washington, more than five million voter ballot packets have already been printed, according to a court filing. Hawaii election officials said in their filing that it would be difficult to order new envelopes “from the continent on such short notice.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread mail voting fraud, even as he voted by mail himself in two elections this year. In part because of those claims, Democrats in recent years have voted by mail in higher numbers than Republicans, which in turn has led opponents to believe that Mr. Trump is looking to control ballot delivery in order to interfere with the results in November.

They also fear that the president’s campaign will sow confusion and mistrust among voters, and prompt some not to vote at all.

While the president has said his purpose is to detect and disqualify ineligible voters to protect the security of U.S. elections, he has also suggested that restrictions on mail voting would help Republicans win elections.

On Thursday, the judge in the Massachusetts case said during a hearing on the matter that the rule, which resulted from an executive order issued by Mr. Trump, could cause “major disenfranchisement” of voters.

Later the same day, the Trump administration made an emergency request to the Supreme Court to clear the way for the new rule, arguing that the lower court’s freeze on the plan imposes “serious irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public.”

However, the emergency request also suggested that ballots that have already been sent to voters might not be subject to the rule change.

“Once those ballot envelopes enter the mail-stream, there is no retrieving them,” wrote D. John Sauer, the solicitor general.

Voters in North Carolina, unlike in many other states, are more likely to cast their ballots in person than they are by mail. Even in 2024, when Hurricane Helene swept away polling locations and displaced voters in the western part of the state, only about 5 percent of voters mailed in their ballots. But that margin could make a difference in a state with a Senate race that is key to the Democratic Party’s hopes of reclaiming the chamber.

State election officials said on Thursday that, whatever the courts decide, they will follow the law.

“It is business as usual as far as I’m concerned,” said Sam Hayes, executive director of the North Carolina Board of Elections, which has a Republican majority, during a news conference on Thursday.

Under the proposed Postal Service rule, the agency would examine ballots and could reject entire batches of up to 10,000 after finding just one ballot error.

Even if the Supreme Court green lights the rule, the federal government may not have time to fully exercise it. Although many states, including North Carolina, already use ballot envelopes that meet the new requirements, the Postal Service does not yet have the technology to screen ballots in the manner the rule would require. The agency has been trying to develop such a system swiftly, but a whistle-blower said this week that the development was rushed and sloppy.

Eileen Sullivan, Richard Fausset and Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

item.title: Photo of Road Runner Snagged by Coyote Shows That Cartoons Were a Lie
item.description:
Cartoons aren’t real.

There. We hate to be the ones to break it to you. But it’s important to establish that rabbits aren’t wisecracking smart-alecks from Flatbush, there is no 12-year-old who can bend the four elements with his mind, and dogs don’t talk (no, not even to say “ruh-roh”).

And, sometimes, the coyote catches the road runner.

In the classic “Looney Tunes” cartoons featuring the Road Runner and Wile E. Coyote, which first appeared in 1949, the coyote is foiled again and again in his efforts to catch the puckish bird in the deserts of the American Southwest.

But a photographer in the Chatsworth Nature Preserve in Los Angeles on Saturday captured a real-life image of something you would never see in that cartoon: a coyote who successfully nabbed a road runner, instead of falling from a cliff, getting hit by a train or having an anvil land on him.

The photographer, Alexander deBarros, snapped the photo while out with a survey team from the San Fernando Valley Audubon Society for a monthly check of the ecosystem at the preserve, a 1,325-acre space in northwestern Los Angeles. (The photograph was reported by the Los Angeles TV news station KTLA.)

There is no indication that this coyote effected the capture through the use of an Acme jet-propelled pogo-stick, Acme rocket-powered roller skates or Acme dehydrated boulders (“Just add water!”).

Also, there were no reports of the road runner saying, “Beep, beep.”

While the image proved that coyotes do sometimes come out on top against road runners, it’s not a common occurrence. “It is considered very rare for a coyote to catch a road runner,” said Scott E. Henke, a professor at the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute at Texas A&M University, Kingsville.

Road runners can run about 20 miles an hour and are agile, he said. “Physically they can outrun a coyote,” he said, and they “can fly up into tree branches to escape attacks.”

Mr. deBarros said in an interview that he initially thought the prey might be a ground squirrel. “When we confirmed that it was, in fact, a road runner in that coyote’s mouth, we freaked out a little bit,” he said. In 17 years of birding, he said, it was the first time he had seen the cartoon antagonists together.

When Mr. deBarros spotted the coyote, it already had the road runner in its mouth. He did not see any chase or kill.

Dr. Henke said this particular road runner might have been caught because it was distracted hunting its own prey, or perhaps it had been hit by a vehicle and was scavenged by the coyote.

Scavenged? Maybe Wile E. didn’t catch the road runner after all.

Another coyote expert, Stanley D. Gehrt, a professor of wildlife ecology at Ohio State University, agreed that the scavenger theory could be true. “But I have learned to never underestimate coyotes,” he said. “They can do anything, even catch a road runner.”

In an odd coincidence, Mr. deBarros’s father, Brian Mainolfi, is an animator who worked with Chuck Jones, a creator of the coyote-road runner cartoons, on the 1994 cartoon “Chariots of Fur.”

Mr. Jones, who died in 2002, once said he got the idea for the coyote character from a travel book by a classic novelist. “I first got interested in the coyote as an animal while perusing Mark Twain’s ‘Roughing It’ at the age of 7,” he said in a 1989 interview with The New York Times. “I thought of it as a sort of dissolute collie. And actually, that’s just about what a coyote is! No one saw it more clearly than Mark Twain.”

The cartoon has been back on the radar since the American release last Friday of the movie “Coyote vs. Acme,” in which the coyote sues the Acme Corporation for its defective products.

(It is fictional.)

(Oh, and by the way, cave men didn’t propel cars made of rocks with their feet, either.)

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: 2 Trump Envoys Headed to Moscow and Kyiv to Revive Peace Talks
item.description:
Two of President Trump’s top envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are traveling to Moscow and Kyiv this weekend, in an effort to revive discussions of a peace agreement to end the four-and-a-half year war in Ukraine.

“They’re bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” Mr. Trump said in the Oval Office on Friday, adding that “there may be a good chance we will do it.”

Mr. Witkoff, the president’s special envoy, and Mr. Kushner, his son-in-law and frequent key negotiator, are expected to see President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Saturday, according to officials familiar with the diplomatic effort. Then they will travel to Kyiv, a first for the two envoys, to see President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Mr. Zelensky confirmed that plan in a social media post on Friday afternoon, saying that Ukraine would temporarily cease drone attacks while the negotiators were in Russia, and called on Mr. Putin to reciprocate by temporarily halting strikes on Ukraine.

“We are looking out for them,” Mr. Zelensky said of Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff. “Not for Russia,” adding that “our goal is to make the visit and the talks with the U.S. side as constructive and substantive as possible.”

Negotiations over the trip have gone on for weeks, said the officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a trip that had not yet been formally announced.

It is unclear whether the Americans are bringing new proposals to the two presidents, or are pushing them to close the gap on the remaining issues, which include who will ultimately control the Donbas, Ukrainian territory that is partly occupied by Russia. When a reporter asked Mr. Trump on Friday if his negotiators were bringing new proposals, he cut her off and quickly said “no” and suggested that the primary obstacle to peace was a “personality problem” between Mr. Putin and Mr. Zelensky.

“They truly hate each other,” he said. “They have serious hate, and it is getting in the way of them.”

While Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner have traveled to Moscow several times, they have not been to Kyiv, despite multiple official invitations. Two weeks ago the C.I.A. director, John Ratcliffe, traveled to Moscow, staying only a few hours to meet with his Russian counterpart. Mr. Witkoff has seen Mr. Putin more than a half-dozen times.

The meeting comes at a precarious moment in the conflict. For most of the year, Ukraine’s attacks on oil refineries and other energy targets have had a devastating effect, leaving Russians lining up for hours to get gasoline, if they can find it at all. But the Ukrainians have run out of interceptors to stop Russian missiles that have been raining down on Ukraine, leaving Kyiv and some other cities almost defenseless.

Mr. Trump has been eager to bring Russia back into the fold: He and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent invited Russia to participate in a Group of 20 finance ministers meeting last week in North Carolina, over the objections of European allies. Russia has been excluded from many diplomatic meetings since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

The session comes more than a year after Mr. Trump met Mr. Putin in a summit meeting in Alaska, the administration’s highest-level effort to end the war. Ever since that session, Russian and U.S. officials have disputed what, exactly, the two men said about the outlines of a possible agreement.

And the Ukrainians were somewhat relieved at that deadlock: Desperate as they were to end the death and destruction, their deepest fear was that Mr. Trump would give in to the Russian president’s territorial demands, and force Mr. Zelensky into a painful choice between giving up more than 20 percent of his country or rejecting a peace accord that he fears is a poison chalice.

The dynamic has changed since. But it is far from clear that Mr. Putin, despite the pressure on Russian energy and the economy, is prepared to give ground on his territorial demands. Some Ukrainian officials say they doubt the conditions will be ripe for a peace agreement until next spring because they expect the Russians will want to use the winter months to try to destroy more of their energy facilities in hopes of making the Ukrainians more malleable.

item.title: A More Confident Iran Emerges After Six Months of War With the U.S.
item.description:
Iran has grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East and appears determined to continue the conflict for months to frustrate the United States, according to U.S. intelligence reports in recent weeks.

In many respects, the assessments reflect what has been observable on the ground as fighting erupted again after a period of relative calm. In the past week, Iran targeted ships in the Strait of Hormuz and American troops in the region, and U.S. forces struck inside Iran, killing military personnel and civilians.

The new exchanges have been limited so far. But the intelligence reports, according to people who have read them, suggest that Iran’s hard-line government might be contemplating a significant escalation.

Iran has emerged from months of the on-again, off-again war with a far better understanding of its military strengths and is more sure of its capabilities, according to officials briefed on the intelligence.

The reports, some current and former officials said, suggest that any agreement to fully end the war will be hard to reach. There are few signs that Iran is ready to make any sort of deal with the United States, content to exacerbate President Trump’s political problems ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, according to some officials.

Mr. Trump, for now, is not pursuing negotiations and has said he believes he can apply economic pressure on Iran that would force Tehran to make concessions on its control of the strait and perhaps, eventually, its nuclear program. But in the short term, U.S. economic sanctions are likely to continue to provoke escalation, according to officials who have read the intelligence reports.

In the coming weeks, Iran could take actions akin to what it did in July, according to U.S. officials. At that time, Iran attacked American military bases in the Middle East, killing three Americans in Jordan; struck shipping in the Strait of Hormuz; and struck infrastructure in Kuwait and elsewhere.

U.S. officials also believe that Iran-linked hackers were most likely responsible for cyberattacks on more than 100 water systems throughout the United States in late July. Though there were no indications any system was degraded in a way that made water unsafe to drink, the attacks in some cases led to disruptions that required manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories.

Current and former officials said the hackers have also shown interest in attacking American oil and gas infrastructure, though those systems are generally seen as harder to penetrate. It is not clear whether any energy systems have been breached.

There are signs that Iran-linked hackers may have regrouped in recent months after sustaining some losses at the start of the war, according to current and former U.S. officials.

Even absent serious disruptions, cyberattacks are likely to remain an appealing way for Iran to seek to undermine public support in the United States for an already unpopular war, former intelligence officials and security experts said.

Alex Orleans, a former U.S. government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, said Iran’s cyberoperators probably feel emboldened. “Even if such attacks fail to meaningfully unsettle the American public, they can still play into a broader effort to exhaust domestic patience with this administration’s handling of the conflict,” he said.

At a news briefing on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance appeared to acknowledge that such attacks could further erode support for a conflict that has no clear end in sight. He sought to downplay the threat to Americans, but said the Trump administration expected Tehran to continue to “try to do a lot of things” to target the United States.

“If you look at the Iranian ability to disrupt the normal lives of Americans, I think it is quite limited,” Mr. Vance said, responding to a reporter’s question about cyberattacks. “It’s not zero, but it’s quite limited. I’d be much more worried about cyberattacks from other actors.”

Mr. Trump predicted a quick and decisive victory as U.S. and Israeli forces launched the war on Feb. 28. After waves of punishing attacks, the president’s critics say it is painfully clear that the Trump administration underestimated Iran’s resilience.

“Iranians are feeling pretty bullish about their position,” said Representative Jason Crow, Democrat of Colorado and a member of the Intelligence Committee. “They have taken substantial damage, but that has always been built into their system. They understand they can take damage, and they are playing a much longer game here.”

Mr. Crow declined to comment on classified assessments, but he said the Iranians believe that they are in a stronger position for several reasons. First, he said, Iran’s formerly splintered leadership is now more united, and the internal opposition has been silenced. Iran also continues to have a stockpile of missiles and drones.

Iran’s leadership also appears to have a more precise understanding of how to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, which carried one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war.

“They have always known the strait was a big bargaining chip, but have come to realize to a greater degree the leverage that gives them,” Mr. Crow said.

Others briefed on the reports said Iran probably believes that the U.S. military will be hard pressed to mount major new strikes as its munitions stockpiles dwindle.

And there are signs that Iran is intent to drag out the conflict until at least the midterms, current and former officials said.

Iran, according to officials, understands that the war — and the high gas prices that closing the strait has caused — is politically damaging to Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

“The Iranians think they have maximum leverage,” said Representative Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey. “So, from their perspective, why not keep sticking it to the president?”

There are indications that Iran is seeking to spread propaganda that would undermine Mr. Trump electorally, as it did during the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. Last week, Meta released a report highlighting a small network of accounts on Facebook and Instagram originating in Iran that focused on U.S. politics. The network’s content, some of which was generated with artificial intelligence, included “anti-Republican views,” Meta said.

Alethea, a threat intelligence company, said domestic media in Iran had published more than 1,200 Persian-language articles within the past two weeks referring to both Mr. Trump and the midterms. The dominant framing, Alethea said, was that the war had become a political liability for Mr. Trump.

Mr. Gottheimer, another member of the Intelligence Committee who declined to discuss classified reports, said he initially supported the war. But he said that the Trump administration has not had a clear strategy, and that Iran has been able to shake off the attacks.

“Because the Iranian government does not care much about the suffering of its people, it has been able to withstand both punishing economic sanctions and military bombardments,” he said.

item.title: ‘It Was Insulting’: When Steinem Said Young Women Backed Sanders to Chase Men
item.description:
Remember the time the world’s most famous feminist implied that young women liked Bernie Sanders more than Hillary Clinton basically because they wanted to chase men?

Probably not.

But in February 2016, Gloria Steinem, who died on Wednesday, went on “Real Time With Bill Maher” and made a statement that seemed decidedly sexist.

Mr. Maher asked Ms. Steinem about Mr. Sanders’s outsize support during his presidential campaign from young voters — including young women.

“When you’re young, you’re thinking: ‘Where are the boys? The boys are with Bernie,’” Ms. Steinem said.

It was, in retrospect, a weird time, 10 years and forever ago.

Conventional wisdom said Donald Trump would never become the Republican nominee, let alone the president, let alone twice. Conventional wisdom said Mr. Sanders, the democratic socialist insurgent and independent senator from Vermont, surely would soon fade in his race against Mrs. Clinton — seen as the Democrats’ inevitable pick, and probably the first female commander in chief.

Back then, many people struggled to see the tectonic shifts underway — much less explain them. Still, from Ms. Steinem, the embodiment of the modern women’s movement and a self-described “entrepreneur of social change,” the comment made for an unexpected assessment.

“It was insulting,” Nina Turner, one of Mr. Sanders’s most prominent and vociferous surrogates in his 2016 campaign, said in an interview on Thursday.

“Both to the senator and his policy positions that are very good for women, and also insulting to the women,” said Ms. Turner, a former Ohio state senator. “As if they were just some airhead ditties who were just out searching for men, and the best way to get them was to support Senator Bernie Sanders, or go to his rallies and flirt.”

Navigating gender politics was a persistent theme in that election, even beyond Ms. Steinem’s entry into the debate. Many of Mr. Sanders’s supporters were derogatorily called “Bernie Bros” for their aggressive online attacks against female reporters and supporters of Mrs. Clinton.

Ms. Steinem had been a consistent and outspoken supporter of Mrs. Clinton — in her first presidential bid in 2008, and in her second run in 2016, too.

Critics ignored the broader context of her appearance on Mr. Maher’s show.

Ms. Steinem said that young women were “very activist” and “way more feminist” than they had been in the past.

“They’re mad as hell because they’re graduating in debt, and they’re going to earn a million dollars less over their lifetimes to pay it back,” she said.

“Men tend to get more conservative because they gain power as they age, and women get more radical because they lose power as they age,” she said.

But then she said what she said, and she stopped herself and laughed nervously. Mr. Maher pounced.

“Now, if I said that, you’d swat me,” he said, punctuating his remarks with an expletive.

In the ensuing hubbub, Ms. Steinem tried to backtrack and mitigate.

“I misspoke,” she wrote in a post on Facebook. “What I had just said on the same show was the opposite,” she said. “Whether they gravitate to Bernie or Hillary, young women are activist and feminist in greater numbers than ever before.”

“What I was thinking sitting there,” she said in an email to Katha Pollitt, a feminist and polemicist, writing for The Nation, “was that both young women and young men gravitate toward each other, and here, for a shared reason — Bernie makes an economic message like that of Occupy.” (Remember Occupy, the even longer-ago protest movement against wealth disparity?)

“No one is ever smarter from going on Bill Maher,” Ms. Pollitt said in an interview on Thursday. “There’s something about that show that gets people to say kind of extreme and not very careful things.”

Mark Longabaugh, a top strategist on Mr. Sanders’s 2016 campaign, said, “From my perspective, I didn’t see that as some kind of damning comment about Gloria Steinem and her record as a feminist leader.”

“That really wasn’t the political impact of it,” he continued. “It was that her candidate was just getting killed among younger voters, and she was trying to come up with a reason why.”

Mostly undiscussed in the ephemeral dust-up was an equally interesting and arguably more revealing snippet of history: the time the world’s most famous feminist traveled to Vermont — to stump for Mr. Sanders.

In October 1996, he was running for re-election to Congress against a woman, Susan Sweetser, and a featured speaker at a campaign event at the University of Vermont to spotlight his support from women was none other than Ms. Steinem.

In his 1997 book, “Outsider in the House,” Mr. Sanders wrote that Ms. Steinem’s remarks were “both analytic and deeply radical.” He said she told more than 500 people “that it is no accident that there is a feeling of discouragement and disillusionment in America today” because “Republicans, the right wing, the press with its insistence on sensationalism are all powerful forces that are changing the nature of politics.”

“I’m only here,” Ms. Steinem said to the crowd, “to make Bernie Sanders an honorary woman.”

item.title: How to Define the ‘Reasonable’ in Reasonable Doubt
item.description:
The outcome of Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial may hinge on how the jurors understand the concept of reasonable doubt. But the term is “not easily defined,” as the judge explained to the deadlocked group on Thursday.

“Beyond a reasonable doubt” is a high bar — in fact, it is the highest burden of proof within the United States’ legal system. It means prosecutors must make jurors reasonably certain that the defendant is responsible for the crime.

Still, there is some wiggle room. Judge William Sullivan, who is presiding over the Clancy trial, told jurors that “proof beyond a reasonable doubt does not mean proof beyond all possible doubt, for everything in the lives of human beings is open to some possible or imaginary doubt.”

Ms. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has argued that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children because she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she strangled them with exercise bands in 2023.

The prosecutors must show not only that Ms. Clancy killed the children — which she does not deny — but also that she was in control of her actions and could tell right from wrong.

On Thursday, the jurors told the judge that they were at an impasse, with one person at odds with all of the others. Ms. Clancy’s lawyer asked for that juror to be removed for failing to “listen to the law on reasonable doubt,” but his request was declined.

Instead, Judge Sullivan gave the jurors instructions on reasonable doubt and sent them back to the deliberation room.

Under Massachusetts law, judges cannot use their own words to explain reasonable doubt, said R. Michael Cassidy, a law professor at Boston College. That is why the judge read verbatim from instructions that were created by the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in 2015.

“The charge is proved beyond a reasonable doubt if, after you’ve compared and considered all of the evidence,” Judge Sullivan said, “you have in your minds an abiding conviction, to a moral certainty, that the charge is true.”

“Moral certainty,” too, is a tough term to pin down.

“We’re not talking about scientific certainty,” Professor Cassidy said. “We’re talking about moral certainty, and that means an abiding conviction: as firmly convinced as you can be in everyday affairs in your life.”

It is up to the prosecution — not the defense — to meet that high standard of persuasion, as Judge Sullivan reminded the jurors on Thursday.

“If you evaluate all the evidence and you still have a reasonable doubt remaining,” he said, “the defendant is entitled to the benefit of that doubt and must be acquitted.”

item.title: Gloria Steinem Stayed Positive, Even as the Manosphere Took Hold
item.description:
For decades, Gloria Steinem invited women into her Upper East Side apartment, a cozy space packed with mementos from her life as a crusading feminist. The women participated in her famous “talking circles,” shared stories and talked political strategy.

And in recent years, after the fall of Roe v. Wade and the election of Donald Trump, some of the attendees arrived with the expectation that their host would feel as despairing as they did.

“People would walk in and say, ‘God, she’s going to be so depressed,’” said Cindi Leive, an executive producer of “Dear Ms.,” a documentary on the magazine Ms. Steinem co-founded. “This woman is seeing everything she’s worked for crumble all around her.”

But people who were close to Ms. Steinem, who died on Wednesday at 92, said that she was more focused on counting victories than defeats, even in her later years when feminism was dealt a series of bruising setbacks. As reality shows and social media influencers glorifying traditional gender roles help shape popular culture, and access to contraceptives and abortion was abruptly curtailed in many states, Ms. Steinem held a longer view, her friends said.

After she made speeches at college campuses and conferences, she would come back home with stories of the progress that she was seeing around the country, a continuation of the transformations that she helped usher in beginning in the 1970s.

“She felt that battles were unfinished,” said Letty Cottin Pogrebin, who with Ms. Steinem and other women founded Ms. magazine. “But she focused me and everybody else on the future. She really didn’t want to give the tradwives and the manosphere the credit for being long-lasting.”

The morning after Ms. Steinem’s death, tributes from admirers poured in from around the world. Many people credited Ms. Steinem’s activism for creating opportunity, for making it possible for women to choose whatever they wanted with their lives. Her work challenged a status quo that left women vulnerable to domestic violence, with far fewer legal rights than men and scant opportunities in the work force.

“Over the decades, she became one of the architects of the entire structure of women’s equality,” Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state, wrote on social media.

But amid the praise, there were also questions: Was the work she led being slowly undone in recent years? Was Ms. Steinem right to remain stubbornly positive about the future of women’s rights, even as antipathy toward women seems to keep flaring hotter? And maybe most urgently, during this unsteady moment in feminism, should there be someone who can pick up her mantle and lead with authority?

“It’s hard to think that there’s a single person or a single organization” leading the charge, said Debbie Walsh, director of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University, who credited her with broadening the women’s movement across class and race. “There are so many folks writing and thinking about these issues that it’s hard to have any one entity hold up that mantle. Our world is more diffuse.”

Some of feminism’s gains are well established, she said, pointing out that women are running corporations and outnumbering men in law schools. “We’re not talking gender balance, but certainly very different from where it was in the early ’70s,” she said. “Progress has been slow and painful.”

That progress led to successive waves of backlash, from Phyllis Schlafly’s winning campaign against the Equal Rights Amendment to the current manosphere, where there is even debate over whether to remove women’s right to vote.

Still, many younger people have a hard time imagining the sweeping economic, political and social changes could ever be rolled back, said Marcia Ann Gillespie, a former editor of Essence and a longtime editor at Ms magazine.

And in the 2016 campaign, when Mr. Trump promised to appoint judges that would overturn Roe v. Wade, there was not enough urgency among women to address the threat to abortion rights, Ms. Gillespie said. “The kind of energy that would have been needed simply wasn’t there,” she said. “The last thing we can ever do is assume that because something is, it will always be.”

Ms. Steinem shied away from questions of legacy during her lifetime. When people asked her who she was going to “give her torch” to, she found the question irritating.

“I’m keeping my torch. And I’m using it to light other people’s torches,” she said. “Because the whole idea that there is only one torch is the problem.”

That inclination to identify and encourage like-minded activists and thinkers across lines of race, class, age and even sex was a constant in her work long before “intersectionality” became a progressive buzzword, said the writer Susan Faludi.

“For so many years she knitted together the big baggy state of feminism,” Ms. Faludi said. “It was almost an instinct with her.”

Ms. Faludi met Ms. Steinem in the early 1990s, when Ms. Steinem cold-called her soon after the publication of Ms. Faludi’s book, “Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women.” Soon after, they appeared together on the cover of Time magazine, with the headline, “Fighting the Backlash Against Feminism.”

“She just took me under her wing as she did over and over and over with young women,” Ms. Faludi said. “In this very old-fashioned way, she was a mother to the movement.”

When Ms. Gillespie stepped down as editor of Essence magazine in 1980, she said, Ms. Steinem was one of the first people to call, with an invitation to become a contributing writer at Ms.

In 1998, the two women raised money to purchase Ms. magazine from a male entrepreneur. They later crisscrossed the country together, speaking to audiences and raising more funds for the magazine they both loved, with help from Ms. Steinem’s impressive Rolodex.

“She got the fact that not everyone was meant to agree with her and not every woman was automatically a feminist and not all feminists thought alike,” Ms. Gillespie said. “That has proven to be one of the truths of this movement.”

Still, like many magazines, Ms. has fallen in stature and influence as the internet took hold. And some other Steinem-era feminist groups, like the National Women’s Political Caucus, have also frayed over time.

At a shaky moment for the causes and institutions Ms. Steinem devoted her life to, many of the women who were close to her over the years — or were just touched by her — see themselves as part of her legacy.

“She told me, ‘You’re an itinerant feminist organizer, that’s what you are, that’s what we are,’” recalled Shelby Knox, who unexpectedly became Ms. Steinem’s roommate in 2007. Ms. Steinem had offered her home to someone in a young women’s leadership program, while she was away at a summer writer’s retreat.

A week into Ms. Knox’s stay, Ms. Steinem arrived home, having left the retreat early.

Ms. Steinem, then in her 70s, insisted Ms. Knox stay. And even though there was a 50-year age gap, the women became close.

“I always called her my mentor and she hated that,” Ms. Knox remembered. “She was like, ‘No, no, we’re learning from each other.’”

Still, Ms. Steinem gave her plenty of advice: Don’t go to graduate school, don’t be afraid to disagree with your elders — and don’t get discouraged.

“She always reminded me historically of how short a time we had been fighting this fight,” Ms. Knox said. “And the more successful we are, the more backlash there will be.”

item.title: Trump Plans to Use Qatari Jet for Another Overseas Flight Despite Security Concerns
item.description:
President Trump is planning to take the Boeing luxury jet donated by the Qataris when he travels to Ireland next week, the first time he will use the plane overseas since questions were raised about its defensive capabilities, a senior administration official said on Friday.

Mr. Trump said several weeks ago that the plane would be taken out of service for roughly a month for new security upgrades.

The Washington Post reported earlier on Mr. Trump’s plans to use the Qatari plane. A senior White House official, speaking on background, would not comment on specific upgrades to Air Force One.

The plane was retrofitted quickly to be pushed into service for Mr. Trump to use during his current term, after two new jets commissioned from Boeing for presidential travel were badly delayed. But those planes are intended as essentially flying presidential command centers, with extensive capabilities to fend off missile strikes, and they can take a long time to build.

Asked about his travel plans and whether the Qatari jet would still be “maxed out” for security, as he put it weeks ago, the president said on Friday, “Well, it has a lot of stuff, but to max it out, meaning you can go into any territory, it’ll take about 60 days and it’s being sent in October to be maxed out.”

The Qatari jet’s safety capabilities came into question after Mr. Trump last used it on a foreign trip, to the NATO summit in Turkey in July. Mr. Trump declared that he would fly on one of the older presidential aircraft for his departure, instead of the Qatari jet that he had flown into Europe with, for “old time’s sake.”

Multiple people with knowledge of the matter said that there had been a security concern about him flying aboard the Qatari plane. The New York Times reported that the Qatari jet lacked defensive capabilities that the older models have.

People briefed on the matter later said that officials had learned of a threat to the president and Air Force One while they were in Turkey, prompting the switch.

Although he boarded the older plane at the airport in Ankara, Turkey, it later emerged that the president had been whisked off it and onto a military jet, leaving the older Air Force One aircraft as a decoy flight.

Mr. Trump said last year that the Qatari plane would go to his planned presidential library in Miami, which is expected to be a skyscraper with a hotel. Other officials have since said it likely won’t be the plane featured at the museum.

On Friday, Mr. Trump said, “I haven’t made a decision, but it will probably go to the museum. It’s scheduled to go to the museum.”

If it doesn’t go to the museum, a reporter asked, what would you do with it?

Mr. Trump replied after a brief pause, “I think it’s going to the museum.”

item.title: Pentagon Agreement With N.I.H. on Biodefense Draws Alarm From Democrats
item.description:
The Pentagon and the National Institutes of Health have signed an agreement to collaborate on biodefense and pandemic preparedness, drawing criticism from Democrats on Capitol Hill who warned that the plan could allow the Defense Department to go around Congress and gain access to billions of dollars meant for infectious disease research.

The agreement, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, is focused on chemical and biological defense research. It does not specify a dollar figure for the partnership or which research projects would be included, but people familiar with it who spoke on the condition of anonymity said it could involve as much as $2 billion from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, about a third of the agency’s budget.

Congressional Democrats, who publicized the agreement, said they feared it would allow Pentagon officials to spend money lawmakers had allocated for programs at the health agency on their own priorities instead. The Trump administration has repeatedly found ways to go around Congress on spending, including canceling federal grants. It has also used similar arrangements, known as interagency agreements, to try to gut the Education Department by subcontracting its functions to other departments.

“The interagency agreement needs to be terminated immediately,” said Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. “These funds were provided for lifesaving medical research, not as extra money for the Department of Defense.”

Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, accused the Defense Department of “trying to rob N.I.H. of billions of dollars that Congress provided for medical research so that it can pad the Pentagon’s budget.”

Trump administration officials denied that was the case.

Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the N.I.H. director, defended the agreement on Friday, writing on social media that “far from siphoning money away from research, this partnership between @NIH and @DeptofWar focuses on research projects that will drive discoveries to improve the health of American citizens and members of the military.”

“Led by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, all work will be 100% aligned with our public health mission,” Mr. Bhattacharya wrote.

Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said on social media that “the NIH is not transferring any money to the Pentagon. This is a project-by-project research partnership.” He accused Ms. DeLauro of twisting facts about the arrangement to score “political points.”

In a statement, a Pentagon official said that the agreement “represents a significant step forward in protecting the American people and our war fighters,” and “formalizes a productive collaboration” among agencies that Congress had long encouraged.

“The assertion by any official that the agreement was made in secret, or for any other purpose, is false,” the statement said, adding that the deal “does not constitute any blanket transfer of funds.”

The agreement arrives at a moment of turbulence and uncertainty at the infectious disease institute, which has lost many of its longtime leaders and is undergoing major strategic shifts under the Trump administration. The agency is veering away from biodefense and pandemic preparedness research that was once one of its three core areas of focus.

In the journal Nature Medicine this January, N.I.H. leaders set out a new vision for the infectious disease institute, arguing that the agency’s work on pandemic preparedness “clearly neither prevented the pandemic nor prevented Americans from experiencing among the highest levels of all-cause excess mortality in the developed world during that time.”

The infectious disease institute played a leading role in the scientific response to the pandemic, and its longtime director, Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, was the public face of many pandemic policies. The agency was instrumental in the rapid development of vaccines credited with saving millions of lives, but has since become a political lightning rod.

In the past, about a third of the agency’s roughly $6.6 billion budget has been allocated for biodefense and emerging pathogen research. But in a recent strategic plan, the word “biodefense” was absent.

The agreement was signed by Dr. Bhattacharya and Dr. Robert Kadlec at the Defense Department. Dr. Kadlec previously served as assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Department of Health and Human Services and played a central role in Operation Warp Speed, the federal government’s effort to rapidly develop vaccines and therapeutics against Covid-19.

A spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, Madeline Meeker, said in a statement that potential collaborations could “support the development of medical technologies, such as therapeutics, diagnostics and personal protective equipment, to protect against infectious diseases and other health risks that Americans face,” citing the response to the Ebola outbreak as an example.

It comes as the Pentagon has sought to significantly increase its budget. The administration has requested $1.5 trillion, including a $350 billion tranche of funding passed through the partisan reconciliation process.

Both requests are stalled on Capitol Hill. Democrats opposed to the war in Iran have refused to provide more funding to the Pentagon through the bipartisan appropriations process, and Senate Republicans remain divided over the budget plan needed to start the reconciliation process.

Congressional Republicans last year included $150 billion in additional funding for the Pentagon in their major tax and spending cuts legislation.

Helene Cooper contributed reporting.

item.title: In a Last-Ditch Effort, Clancy Lawyer Takes His Case to a Higher Court
item.description:
Just as the judge was about to formally declare a mistrial in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy on Friday morning, her lawyer made an extraordinary appeal for an emergency stay.

It was a last-ditch effort. The judge, William Sullivan, had just announced that he planned to declare a mistrial because the jury had failed to come to unanimous agreement on a verdict.

Ms. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, asked the judge to send the jurors back to deliberation, but that request was denied. A minute passed, and just as the jury was on its way into the courtroom, Mr. Reddington stood up again to try something else.

Referring to the situation as a “travesty,” Mr. Reddington appealed to a Massachusetts law that establishes the “general superintendence” of the state’s supreme judicial court and calls upon it to correct or prevent errors in the lower courts, as long as “no other remedy is expressly provided.”

With some hesitation, Judge Sullivan allowed the emergency stay. “I’ll give you an hour,” he said.

Mr. Reddington was making what is known as an interlocutory appeal, according to R. Michael Cassidy, a law professor at Boston College. Essentially, Mr. Reddington was asking a single justice of the state’s Supreme Judicial Court to prevent the declaring of a mistrial, citing a constitutional rights violation, even though the murder trial has yet to formally conclude.

The justice may allow for a hearing and grant Mr. Reddington’s request, deny it with or without a hearing, or refer the matter to the full bench of the state’s supreme court.

It may be a long shot, but Mr. Reddington’s request is not entirely without precedent. Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts Superior Court judge, said that emergency appeals to a higher court during murder trials are common, and the requests are sometimes granted.

However, he added, he was unaware of any precedent for a lawyer to make the request so soon before a mistrial is declared, and to have a “made-for-TV drama where the judge stops almost in midsentence and stays the case.”

Professor Cassidy said that he doubted Mr. Reddington would succeed. “But apparently the judge is letting him take his Hail Mary shot,” he added.

Jurors have been deliberating since last week for a total of about 38 hours, and they have been deadlocked at least since Tuesday. On Thursday, they revealed that one juror was at odds with all of the others. Mr. Reddington had asked for that juror to be removed, but his request was denied.

item.title: ICE Agent Charged With Six Counts of Lying About Minnesota Shooting
item.description:
Federal prosecutors charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis with lying repeatedly about the circumstances of the incident in an indictment made public on Friday.

The officer, Christian Castro, faces six counts of making false statements in his account of the Jan. 14 shooting. He surrendered to federal authorities on Thursday and appeared before a federal magistrate judge in McAllen, Texas, where he lives, the next morning.

The federal indictment marked a rare instance of the Trump administration seeking to hold an immigration agent accountable for actions taken while on duty.

Soon after the shooting, Mr. Castro told an F.B.I. agent that he fired his service weapon while lying on the ground after enduring a brutal, minutes-long assault by three men, according to the indictment. He told the agent that he had been repeatedly struck with a broom and a shovel before opening fire.

But surveillance video of the episode contradicted the officer’s account. Instead, prosecutors said in the indictment that Mr. Castro had been standing up when he shot a bullet through the front door of the residence and that he made demonstrably false claims about acting in self-defense.

Mr. Castro entered a not guilty plea at Friday’s hearing. The magistrate judge, Juan F. Alanis, set bond at $75,000 and ordered that Mr. Castro wear an ankle monitor, surrender his passport and travel to Minnesota for a Sept. 18 hearing, said Rolando Cantu, a lawyer representing him.

Another lawyer representing Mr. Castro, David A. Lindenmuth, said there had been a rush to judgment in his client’s case.

“It feels like Mr. Castro is bearing the full force of the anger, distress and resentment of the people of Minnesota,” Mr. Lindenmuth, a former federal prosecutor, said.

Mr. Castro had a long career in public service that included wartime service in the Army, Mr. Lindenmuth said. His military service left him with a traumatic brain injury and a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder, conditions Mr. Lindenmuth said led the Veterans Affairs administration to grant him a 100 percent disability rating.

Mr. Castro, 52, joined ICE last September, meaning he had only been an immigration enforcement agent for a few months at the time of the shooting. He has since been suspended without pay.

Mr. Castro also faces a separate set of criminal charges filed in state court in Minneapolis in May. In that case, he was charged with four counts of felony assault with a dangerous weapon and one count of making a false police report.

The state charges led to his arrest in Texas in late May and prompted a rare legal battle over extradition law after Gov. Greg Abbott declined to act on a request from Minnesota officials to extradite Mr. Castro. A federal judge sided with Texas, leading to Mr. Castro’s release from custody last week.

Mary Moriarty, the county prosecutor in Minneapolis who brought the state charges, said she was hopeful the federal charges would lead to Mr. Castro’s return to Minnesota.

“Despite Gov. Abbott’s best efforts to shield Mr. Castro, we will see him soon,” she said in a statement.

Mr. Castro’s account of the shooting was the basis of criminal charges of assaulting a federal agent that were filed against the man he shot, Julio Sosa-Celis, and his roommate. Both men are from Venezuela and did not have legal status at the time of the shooting. The government eventually dismissed that case after reviewing the surveillance video.

The indictment does not address the lawfulness of the shooting itself, which has been a source of debate within the Justice Department in recent weeks. And it did not reveal any new information about how the initial investigation was mishandled.

Career federal prosecutors in Minnesota sought to charge Mr. Castro with civil rights violations, which carry stiffer penalties. But they failed to get sign-off from top officials in Washington.

The disagreement over the charges led the Justice Department to fire one of the prosecutors who oversaw the case after an email the prosecutor wrote expressing his displeasure about the decision came to light earlier this week.

Justice Department officials in Washington said their investigation into the shooting remained open and that civil rights charges could be filed at a later date.

Gabriel V. Cárdenas contributed reporting from McAllen, Texas.
