item.title: The Local: Follow the Ice
item.description:
John Abdo’s family has sold ice for half a century. This year, however, he’s found that some people are taken aback when he mentions his business. It’s ice, not ICE.

“Like, frozen water,” he clarifies. “No affiliation.”

I spent Tuesday afternoon following the Abdos, learning how they deliver innumerable cubes throughout the Minnesota State Fairgrounds on human-powered carts. That story is below, along with visuals from Tim Gruber.

Also today, my colleague Talya Minsberg interviews the fair’s butter sculptor and brings us tips from a St. Paul produce expert. Let’s start with some news.

A history of threats and domestic violence preceded Wednesday’s deadly shooting in Minneapolis. The Star Tribune has the back story.

Minnesota health care providers say immigrant parents remain reluctant to bring their children in for checkups and procedures. The Reformer details the outcomes.

The Strib talked to Prince fans who are furious after finding altered sounds in “Timeless,” which was billed as an album of songs as they were originally recorded. Here’s a review in The Current.

The ICE agent who was arrested in Texas for a January shooting in Minneapolis, Christian Castro, now faces federal charges of lying about the incident. Mr. Castro entered a not guilty plea at Friday’s hearing. My colleague at The Times who has been covering the case notes that it’s rare for the Trump Justice Department to charge an ICE agent — and that prosecutors had pressed for more serious charges.

Sign up here to get The Local delivered to your inbox.

There’s an art to managing the weight of a cart laden with 500 pounds of ice while maneuvering down ramps and through crowds.

On a typical run at the fairgrounds this week, two teenage boys eased said cart down a loading dock ramp: one braced against the front, the other held the rear. When the cart reached the bottom, the boy in back hopped up and dragged a sneaker on the ground for control as the duo executed a tight turn and rode their momentum toward Underwood Street.

They were headed for the Shrimp Shack, one of about 300 vendors that rely on Gopher State Ice to keep them stocked with ice during the 12-day fair. (It’s $6.50 per 20-pound bag for those with accounts.) Since few motorized vehicles are allowed into the fair during operating hours, that means a lot of cart runs.

Depending on the crowd size and the heat, Gopher State distributes about one full semi trailer of ice every day. Much of it is destined for the drinks sold throughout the grounds.

Paul, John and Corey Abdo, all now in their 40s, have been distributing ice at the fair since they were “in utero,” said their mother, Caryl. It started back in the mid-1970s, when their father, Larry, bought a business that held a State Fair ice contract.

Corey was “on the comm” Tuesday, wearing a cowboy hat as he tabulated orders and palmed a radio handset to keep tabs on their delivery status. Behind him was a whiteboard tracking workers, many listed by nickname: “Bones,” “Big Dog,” “Ricochet.”

The ice runners, who number about 25 over the course of the fair, were all boys and young men. Girls in the family have tended to become “pita princesses” and “bacon babes,” as Caryl put it. (The family also owns the fair’s Big Fat Bacon stand, and used to sell Lebanese Pocket Pies.)

Gopher State’s garage-like base, called the House, serves as a hangout for the runners, with bunks suspended from the wall for naps. On Tuesday, the boys sat around snacking and playing games on their phones, until it was time, again, to roll out.

The carts (custom designed by Larry) are loaded loudly, with bags slammed down to facilitate stable stacking. Rolling through the thick crowds, the ice guys are polite but as relentless as sharks, and move surprisingly quickly. Even fairgoers focused on corn dogs or mini doughnuts tend to see the cart and move.

A sense of wonder can be glimpsed on fairgoers’ faces as the mountain of ice rolls through their midst. At one point on Tuesday, a young girl in a pink princess outfit reached out a hand to touch the freezing bags, as if to confirm that they were real.

After decades of experience, the Abdos know when food and drink stands are likely to be low on ice, and send extra bags to encourage the vendors to stock up. The guys write out receipts by hand, then bring the slips back to be tabulated.

“Good ice guys,” Corey said, “come back with no ice.”

Gerry Kulzer considers himself a celebrity for 12 days a year. During that time, he sits in a rotating refrigerator as hoards of people watch him carve 90-pound hunks of butter into sculpted busts of young women.

The butter-carving tradition at the Minnesota State Fair dates back to 1965. It accompanies a competition, organized by the Midwest Dairy Association, to celebrate so-called dairy princesses across the state. Each year, 10 finalists have their likeness carved into butter. Only one wears the coveted crown as “Princess Kay of the Milky Way.”

Kulzer, an art teacher at Eden Valley-Watkins High School, said he loves his summer gig. Talya spoke to him on the phone:

How did you get this gig?

When I was in college in the early ’90s, I went to the fair and I would watch Linda [Christensen] carve. It was extraordinary. I later contacted Midwest Dairy and said, if she retires, maybe consider me? What I thought was an interview, years later, turned into more of an audition. They gave me 90 pounds of butter and said “there you go, see what you can do.”

The place were you work is kept at 40 degrees Fahrenheit. How do you survive in there all day?

Being in the butter booth is like working in your fridge at home. Your fingers lose dexterity as they freeze. I wear two layers of gloves, and that’s difficult too; you don’t have as much control with gloves on. It’s so chilly — even when it’s 90 degrees outside — so I look for any hot food for lunch. You can’t go wrong with anything fresh out of the broiler.

Have you done butter sculptures outside of the fair?

It’s surprising how many different weird commissions people ask for. One of the most memorable was when someone wanted a Minnesota loon, life-size, for their Thanksgiving table.

One of the former Princess Kay finalists had their block of butter in the freezer and they were getting married. They wanted a butter head for their future husband, so I got to carve the fiancé. Then they displayed both at the wedding.

Here are details on our next fair appearance, and more tips for what to do this weekend.

Are you a Wordle fan? Join me and my co-host, Shadi Bushra, on Saturday at the Strib booth, when we invite fairgoers to play a live version of the game at 9 a.m., 1 p.m. and 4 p.m. Yes, there will be prizes.

A collaborative 21-foot artwork in the style of Pablo Picasso’s “Guernica,” commenting on the ICE surge last winter, is the centerpiece of an exhibit now at FindFurnish. Thanks to Sahan Journal, which also documented a “Guernica” remix in State Fair crop art, for this recommendation; subscribe here to their Pathfinder newsletter.

Southside Back in the Day is an annual community festival anchored in a celebration of South Minneapolis history, including its time as a center for the Black community, its organizer Lisa Crawford told City Cast Twin Cities. This year’s event takes place Saturday at Phelps Park.

It’s the last weekend of summer. Look for tomatoes. Any tomatoes, really.

“The one thing thriving in this dry summer has been tomatoes,” Lindsay Stauner, the assistant director of the St. Paul Growers Association, told Talya.

She estimates there are some 15 to 20 varieties available across the 20 markets under the association’s umbrella. There are heirloom varieties, plus cherry, slicing, Roma, beefsteak and variegated.

She especially recommends the heirlooms. Look for ones that have yellows and touches of greens and dark maroons. “The most gorgeous produce you can visualize,” she said.

Here’s a tomato vinaigrette salad from NYT Cooking that’s perhaps too easy to even call a recipe. Pair it with a side of sourdough bread (if you are coming from the flagship farmers market in downtown St. Paul, stop at Razava Bread Co. on Grand.)

This is also a good time to collect tomatoes to start canning. They’re easy to preserve, as you don’t need to fuss with pickling or fermenting, Stauner said. This preserved crushed tomato recipe is a classic.

There’s a heat advisory for the Twin Cities starting today at 1 p.m., with heat index values as high as 97. Temperatures will remain elevated tomorrow. Stay hydrated and watch for signs of heat exhaustion or heat stroke. Sunday and Labor Day should be cooler, with possible showers.

In April, when social media feeds were full of Coachella, Sierra Nicole Reece, a content creator on the East Coast, posted a video saying she was hoping for a sponsored trip to the Minnesota State Fair instead.

Responses flooded in, and Reece got her wish, courtesy of the fair, Explore Minnesota and Visit Saint Paul. I caught up with Reece afterward and asked her why she wanted to come.

“The fair is so unapologetically Minnesotan,” she observed, “and it’s so unapologetically itself.”

Her favorite food stop? Jive Turkey. Overall impression? “Really good vibe,” she said, calling the fair a “really positive monoculture.”

Have a wonderful Labor Day weekend. We will be on holiday, too. See you Wednesday!

Sign up here if you don’t already get this newsletter delivered to your inbox.

Are you on WhatsApp? Join us there, too, to keep up with us between sends.

Feedback? Questions? We’d love to hear from you: thelocalTC@nytimes.com

item.title: Lindsay Clancy’s Murder Trial Ended With a Hung Jury. What Now?
item.description:
The murder trial of Lindsay Clancy ended on Friday in a mistrial, after the jury failed to come to a unanimous agreement on whether she should be held criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children.

A mistrial is neither an acquittal nor a conviction. The murder charges against Ms. Clancy remain, and it is possible that prosecutors will try their case all over again.

Here is what we know about what happens next:

The Plymouth County district attorney, Timothy J. Cruz, will now decide whether to try Ms. Clancy again in front of a different jury, for first-degree murder or less serious charges. It could take a week or more for prosecutors to consider their options, experts have said.

The prosecutors’ decision will hinge on several factors, including what they learn about the jury’s deliberations. If more jurors were leaning toward an acquittal, a retrial on the same charges might be less likely.

If prosecutors lower the charges against Ms. Clancy — by charging her with second-degree murder, for example — that would open the door to a bench trial, in which the judge delivers a verdict without a jury. It could also lead to a plea deal.

Mr. Cruz is a hard-charging prosecutor who has served in the position for almost 25 years and is now running unopposed for re-election.

Kevin Reddington, Ms. Clancy’s lawyer, said that he “absolutely” expected the district attorney to try her for first-degree murder again, based on Mr. Cruz’s history and reputation.

Even though she was not convicted, Ms. Clancy is not likely to go free.

Her lawyers have claimed that she is not criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she used exercise bands to strangle them, and some experts at the trial have argued that she had bipolar disorder.

She is currently held at Tewksbury Hospital, a state-run facility with inpatient psychiatric care, and she will almost certainly remain there, or at a similar facility in Massachusetts.

If she is not retried in criminal court, experts say that she will probably face civil commitment proceedings, which could keep her at the facility for the foreseeable future.

Mr. Reddington has said that he doesn’t think Ms. Clancy is emotionally prepared to endure another trial, but that he would continue to represent her.

The 12 jurors and six alternate jurors, who have not been publicly named, will be free to go home now that the trial is over. If there is a retrial, they would not be called to serve again; instead, the court would have to find a new group of jurors.

That will be challenging, since Ms. Clancy’s trial has attracted national attention and prompted demonstrations at the courthouse in Plymouth, Mass. Any jurors too familiar with the particulars of this case are likely to be dismissed.

Mr. Reddington has said that if prosecutors try Ms. Clancy again, he would expect a retrial to begin in six months to a year.

Prosecutors could use that time to review their legal strategy and possibly change it. They may need to enter more evidence, volley with defense lawyers over disclosures and pretrial motions, select new witnesses and prepare those witnesses for the stand.

Another recent, closely observed murder case in Massachusetts resulted in a mistrial and eventually a new trial. That case involved a woman, Karen Read, who was accused of killing her boyfriend, a Boston police officer, by hitting him with her vehicle in 2022. She was charged with murder, but the trial ended with a hung jury in July 2024.

It took nine more months for Ms. Read’s retrial to begin, in April 2025. She was ultimately found not guilty of murder.

Ms. Clancy does not deny that she killed her three children at her home in Duxbury, Mass., an affluent Boston suburb, on Jan. 24, 2023.

But she pleaded not guilty to murder, pursuing an insanity defense. Her lawyer maintained that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and had hallucinated a man’s voice ordering her to kill her children and then herself.

Prosecutors argued that Ms. Clancy plotted to get her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the house on the day of the killings. Mr. Clancy said during testimony that he had returned home from running errands to find the children in the basement with exercise bands around their necks. Cora, 5, and Dawson, 3, were dead. Callan, 8 months, died days later.

After listening to four weeks of emotional and sometimes harrowing witness testimony, jurors deliberated for nearly 40 hours. They twice told the judge, William Sullivan, that they were deadlocked, and he urged them to continue.

But on Friday, they said one last time that they could not come to a unanimous agreement, and Judge Sullivan declared a mistrial.

item.title: Clancy Prosecutor Said He Has Not Decided Whether to Retry Case
item.description:
Timothy Cruz, the prosecutor who will decide whether to retry Lindsay Clancy in the 2023 killings of her three children, could have chosen a more lenient path.

He brought first-degree murder charges in a trial that ended Friday with a hung jury. Options included lesser charges or accepting an insanity defense.

But Mr. Cruz, the Plymouth County district attorney prosecuting the Clancy case, went with the most conservative choice, according to lawyers and observers, an approach he has taken for more than two decades as the lead prosecutor in a working-class county.

After the judge declared a mistrial on Friday, Mr. Cruz said he had not yet made a decision about whether to retry the case against Ms. Clancy, dismissing the suggestion that the case was about mental health issues and saying the trial was “about getting justice for those three little babies.”

Mr. Cruz has been uncompromising. During the trial, his office described Ms. Clancy as “selfish” and “calculated,” arguing that she had plotted to get her then-husband out of the house before choking the children.

“Our priority has always been to fight for Cora, for Dawson and for Callan,” Mr. Cruz said on Friday.

Ms. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, with her lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. But prosecutors disputed that view.

Robert F. Shaw, a criminal defense lawyer, said Mr. Cruz’s office “reflexively pursues the harshest charges.”

Mr. Cruz has served as Plymouth County district attorney since 2001. He is a former president of the National District Attorneys Association, where he currently serves as chairman. Mr. Cruz, a Republican, is up for re-election in November but is uncontested.

Jennifer Webb-McRae, the president of the association, said in a statement that Mr. Cruz “represents the very best of what it means to be a prosecutor,” adding that he “understands that this job is more than trying cases, it’s about building trust with the community, working collaboratively with law enforcement, and never losing sight of the people affected by crime.”

Mr. Cruz recently prosecuted another case with parallels to the Clancy case. In that case, Latarsha Sanders, 51, was convicted in 2022 for stabbing two of her children. Like Ms. Clancy, Ms. Sanders pleaded not guilty.

Earlier this month Mr. Cruz faced a setback. The state’s Supreme Judicial Court ordered a retrial, after lawyers for Ms. Sanders argued that the defense should have been able to introduce medical records that documented her mental illness.

The same judge presided over both cases.

Mr. Cruz’s other high-profile cases include solving two decades-old cold cases. Mr. Cruz has made targeting gang and organized crime a priority.

He has also supported the commutation of a first-degree murder sentence for a man who was an accomplice in a robbery that ended in murder.

Mark Arsenault contributed reporting.

item.title: Kennedy Hires Covid Vaccine Skeptic to Look at Dubious Claims of Military Deaths
item.description:
The Department of Health and Human Services has hired an Army doctor with a history of questioning the safety of Covid vaccines to investigate unsubstantiated claims that more than 2,500 U.S. service members died after receiving the shots.

The hiring of Lt. Col. Theresa Long, who has no specialized training in vaccines or viruses, is part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s intense campaign to explore long-held and baseless theories about the hazards of vaccines.

There is little evidence to support this latest investigation. More than 96 percent of service members were vaccinated against Covid before a mandate that they receive the shots was rescinded. A March report from the Pentagon, and one in July 2025, found no deaths from the vaccines.

Dr. Long said in an Aug. 14 legal deposition obtained by The New York Times that she is a senior medical military adviser to Mr. Kennedy but also reports to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

She said in the deposition that she had been appointed to investigate 55,000 reports of adverse effects and 2,544 deaths among service members who received Covid vaccines, in the federal Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System. Experts have noted that while this database is the largest, it is also the least reliable: Reports of side effects can be submitted by anyone and are not vetted, so they may be subject to bias or manipulation.

Dr. Long’s role was reported earlier by Politico. She and H.H.S. did not respond to requests for comment or clarification on the project.

Billions worldwide have received Covid vaccines. The vast majority have experienced no serious side effects, and research has found deaths from the vaccines to be exceedingly rare.

“I have not seen any convincing reports that large numbers of people have died due to the vaccine,” said Dr. Ofer Levy, the director of the precision vaccines program at Boston Children’s Hospital.

Dr. Long testified that she had personal knowledge of the deaths of 28 service members as a result of Covid vaccines. She also said that she knew of several service members who lost pregnancies after receiving Covid shots, and that the vaccines had caused pregnancy loss at a rate of about 82 percent. Studies in hundreds of thousands of women have shown that Covid vaccination is not linked to an increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth.

Dr. Long also echoed inaccurate comments from Mr. Kennedy suggesting that vaccines may cause autism and contending that autism is “extraordinarily rare” in some groups like the Amish who often do not immunize their children. Dozens of studies have explored and dismissed those theories. Last week, Pennsylvania announced two deaths from measles, both in infants from the Amish community.

The 2026 Pentagon report concluded that Covid vaccinations caused a short-term rise in heart inflammation within 21 days — a known side effect — but that the inflammation did not persist, and Covid itself carried a larger risk of the complication. The Defense Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The report also found that Covid vaccines decreased the incidence of eight conditions, including life-threatening ones such as acute kidney failure and hemorrhagic stroke.

Dr. Long told lawyers in the deposition that the Pentagon report cherry-picked data and that she had been appointed specifically to investigate “inaccuracies” in defense databases. She said she hoped to complete her investigation within a year.

Dr. Levy said given the military includes many young men, the group at highest risk of myocarditis, or heart inflammation, from Covid vaccines, he supported research into the safety of the shots in that population. But many infections, including Covid and flu, can cause myocarditis, he noted, and proving the exact cause of death can be exceedingly difficult.

A detailed investigation would require autopsy reports, including samples of nasal passages and lung fluid, and information on any infections the person may have had. “You’d want all of that and more to really reach a very serious conclusion that this is caused by the vaccine,” he said.

Dr. Long’s testimony was part of a defamation lawsuit brought against Ivan Raiklin, a far-right activist, by Dr. Terry Adirim, who as a senior Pentagon health official had advised that military personnel receive Covid shots. Shortly after she moved to a new post at the C.I.A., Mr. Raiklin accused her on social media of committing “jab genocide” with that advice.

In her deposition, Dr. Long spoke in support of Mr. Raiklin and said in immunizing service members, Dr. Adirim was morally comparable to Nazi doctors who were hanged for experimenting on prisoners in concentration camps during World War II.

Dr. Long said she did not receive the Covid vaccine or immunize her two children against the disease. She said she had received every vaccine the military required of her before then, but had struggled with infertility and heart failure.

“And so having received, you know, probably four or five rounds of vaccines every time they lost my vaccine card, I wouldn’t — I wouldn’t say that I feel like those vaccines helped in any way,” she said.

Helene Cooper contributed reporting, and Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Homeland Security Dept. Asks for Inquiries Into Voting Machines
item.description:
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, has asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine can be trusted to create a verifiable record, in what appeared to be the Trump administration’s latest effort to cast doubt on digital voting systems.

In a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche on Wednesday, Mr. Mullin asked the Justice Department to determine whether devices that tally votes through bar codes or QR codes provided what he described as a “reliable record for a manual audit.”

The letter, which asked Mr. Blanche for his department’s help in ensuring that machines known as ballot-marking devices comply with federal law, raises questions about whether the request sought to lay the ground for claiming that some electronically cast or counted votes are invalid.

Unlike the process of voting by handwritten ballot, ballot-marking devices rely on ballots printed from a touch-screen computer. The ballots, which typically designate a voter’s choice in text form and in a bar code or QR code, are then fed into a separate machine that reads the information.

Critics of the devices have claimed that hackers could in theory manipulate the digital codes, though election integrity experts say there are no examples of that happening in an election. The devices have been widely used in states like Georgia and South Carolina, where Mr. Trump has won elections.

Election machines are already heavily monitored and regulated through testing and certification by federal agencies, states, local election offices and private labs. (The Trump administration recently forced out the independent members of the Election Assistance Commission, which oversees the certification of machines.)

In his letter to Mr. Blanche, Mr. Mullin asked the Justice Department to investigate another pillar of the country’s election infrastructure: a multistate partnership called the Electronic Registration Information Center, or ERIC.

ERIC, a database-sharing consortium that helps states ensure that people vote in only one location, was once considered a wonky, bipartisan initiative to help states clean their voter rolls. But in recent years, it has become a target of election conspiracy theorists trying to sow doubt in the process of administering elections.

In his letter, Mr. Mullin indicated that the requests had initially been made to the Justice Department under his predecessor, Kristi Noem, who was ousted in March. The letter, which congratulated Mr. Blanche on being confirmed as attorney general last month, appeared to be an attempt to nudge him into action less than 60 days before the midterm elections.

The Department of Homeland Security said it had no comment beyond Mr. Mullin’s letter.

President Trump has long complained about electronic voting systems, falsely claiming that they were used in a sprawling plot to rig the 2020 election against him. In March 2025, just two months after he returned to the White House, he issued an executive order in which he “raised the issue of the security of voting systems that rely on bar codes and QR codes,” Mr. Mullin noted in his letter.

Mr. Trump reprised his attacks against these machines in a prime-time address two months ago, saying they were “vulnerable” and “easily compromised.” The president pointed to a trove of declassified intelligence documents to make his case, especially those related to a technology company called Smartmatic, which he said had ties to the Venezuelan government.

But Mr. Trump’s claims about Smartmatic’s devices far outran the problems with them that were described in the declassified materials. One of the documents, a C.I.A. analysis, said that while the Venezuelan government had “some capability in manipulating electronic voting systems,” neither it nor Smartmatic could “manipulate the outcome of an election outside Venezuela.”

Mr. Mullin’s letter did not mention Smartmatic by name. But it did refer to an effort last winter by senior Trump intelligence officials to examine the vulnerabilities of machines built by another company, Dominion Voting Systems, now known as Liberty Vote, which has also been at the center of outlandish conspiracy theories.

Conspiracy theories have also long underpinned the conservative efforts to dismantle ERIC. In the aftermath of the 2020 election, election deniers successfully pressured secretaries of state in many Republican states to withdraw from ERIC, claiming it was a front for left-wing groups to organize voter-registration drives.

Those claims were largely promoted by Heather Honey, then a researcher and activist who is now a top official at the Department of Homeland Security working with Cleta Mitchell, a conservative lawyer who played a role in Mr. Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election. Ms. Honey presented a report to several Republican secretaries of state in the summer of 2022 claiming ERIC was inappropriately influenced by partisan Democrats and left-wing groups.

As a result, nine Republican-led states withdrew from ERIC. But nearly 30 states now still use the system.

ERIC is currently the only system that can reliably catch whether people vote in more than one state. And election officials widely agree that it also helps to identify dead people on voting lists.

Mr. Mullin’s letter suggested that data from ERIC, including “protected motor vehicle data,” had been with an organization called the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that works to build confidence in elections. Mr. Mullin told Mr. Blanche that sharing such information with a nongovernmental organization could violate federal privacy laws.

The Center for Election Innovation and Research is run by David Becker, a former voting rights lawyer for the Justice Department who also helped to found the ERIC system. Mr. Becker has vehemently criticized the Trump administration’s attempts to interfere with elections, raising questions about whether the request to investigate ERIC was also an effort to target him and his group.

Mr. Becker said in a statement on Friday that the allegation from Mr. Mullin likely related to research his organization performed over five years ago. Mr. Becker also rejected claims made by Mr. Mullin that the organization received motor vehicle or voter data on an ongoing basis.

“There have been multiple public documents published as far back as early 2022 relating to this research,” the statement said, adding that no one from the Department of Homeland Security contacted the center for “information or clarification” before Mr. Mullin issued his letter.

item.title: Justice Department Issues Subpoenas for Voter Data in Nevada
item.description:
The Justice Department has subpoenaed the Nevada secretary of state for voter information, according to a person familiar with the operation, at a time when the government is rapidly escalating efforts to prove President Trump’s baseless claims of voter fraud.

The office of Cisco Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state and its chief election officer, confirmed receiving seven “voter-related” subpoenas from F.B.I. agents over the last three months, but declined to offer details.

It is unclear whether other states have received similar subpoenas. The U.S. attorney in Nevada, Sigal Chatta, whose office would have overseen the request, is a pro-Trump prosecutor who has repeatedly sought to cast doubt on the integrity of federal elections.

With less than 60 days to go before the midterm elections, the Trump administration has deployed hundreds of investigators to hunt for voter fraud, despite decades of evidence that it is exceptionally rare in the United States. The administration is also aggressively trying to shape how the midterm elections are run, demanding private voter information across the country and seeking to change election rules.

“The right to vote is written clearly in the Constitution, and we cannot take that right away without the highest confidence of a person’s ineligibility,” Mr. Aguilar said in a statement. “The federal administration is inundating election offices with investigations and questions ahead of the election, and making sweeping claims of election fraud to the public before any investigation is done. We will continue standing up for Nevada voters and remain focused on running a safe, secure and transparent election this fall.”

Roughly two dozen states have sued the administration over some of those actions. The Constitution empowers the states and Congress, not the executive branch, with authority to regulate elections.

The subpoenas follow previous efforts by the Justice Department to obtain private voter information in Nevada and elsewhere. In December, the Justice Department sued Nevada and 29 other states, demanding that they hand over private, unredacted voter files. Judges have tossed 23 of these lawsuits, including the one in Nevada.

Separately, the administration has asked the Supreme Court to bless its efforts to restrict mail voting through the U.S. Postal Service, and has enlisted multiple federal agencies in a broad effort to ferret out evidence of ineligible noncitizens on the voter rolls. A study by the conservative Heritage Foundation spanning a quarter-century revealed roughly 100 cases of noncitizen voting nationwide.

The focus on noncitizens has been led largely by the Department of Homeland Security, which has embarked on a weekslong hunt for ineligible immigrants among the nation’s registered voters. Hundreds of its agents have been pulled from their normal duties to scour a data set of names in search of illegal voting histories.

The establishment of a federal voter database has long been a goal of the Trump administration, spanning multiple agencies. Last year, the Justice Department began quietly attempting to build a national voter file. Also last year, the Department of Homeland Security began sending invitations to state election officials encouraging them to upload voter data on a mass scale — including full name, date of birth and Social Security numbers — to an immigration verification tool known as the SAVE system. The administration has also, for the first time, begun using data from the Social Security Administration.

A spokesperson from the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Nevada, a presidential swing state that is hosting a race for governor and one potentially competitive congressional race, has been a particular focus of the administration. In July, the state was one of four highlighted by Mr. Trump during a prime time address as having thousands of noncitizens on the voter rolls. The president offered no evidence at the time to back up his claims.

The administration claimed to have identified 278,000 noncitizens registered to vote in four states, including an exact number of 15,903 in Nevada. But during a meeting last month with state election administrators, Homeland Security officials were unable to substantiate those claims and said they had identified just 185 potential noncitizens in the state so far, according to emails as well as recordings of the meeting obtained by The New York Times.

The nearly 16,000 they had originally identified represented “the ceiling” of potential noncitizens, a D.H.S. official said during the meeting.

item.title: Supreme Court Sides With Republicans in TV Ad Fight
item.description:
In a victory for Republicans in the run-up to the midterms, the Supreme Court on Friday found that political parties are entitled to the same low-cost TV ad rates as candidates.

The ruling focused on an obscure but crucial part of political campaign funding that has given Democrats an advantage in recent years.

The court’s majority found that Republican Party committees were likely to suffer “irreparable harm” unless the justices cleared the way for them to receive the low-cost ad rates, saying that requiring party committees to pay more for advertising would hamper “their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the midterms.”

The majority added that such an injury “implicates their First Amendment rights to speak and coordinate their political activities freely.”

As is typical in such emergency applications, the order did not include a vote count. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the court’s liberals, dissented.

Republican leaders praised the court’s ruling.

A spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, Will Kiley, called the decision “a win for candidates, parties and broadcasters who have relied on the same rules for years.”

He added: “Democrats can’t win at the ballot box, so they ran to the courthouse in the final weeks of an election to try to limit protected party speech.”

Democratic counterparts pushed back against Friday’s ruling.

A joint statement from senior officials with Democrats’ congressional campaign committees called the Republicans’ move “a concerted effort by Donald Trump and national Republicans to flood the midterm elections with money from billionaire donors.” The officials, Devan Barber and Will Van Nuys, added that Republicans were seeking to “drown out the power of the grass roots because they know their agenda is deeply unpopular and they cannot win on the merits.”

The dispute focuses on the 1971 Federal Election Campaign Act, which set out rules for how broadcasting stations must interact with political candidates during election seasons.

The federal law requires broadcasters to give political candidates low rates to buy TV ad time in the weeks before an election — a key way to reach voters. Before the court’s ruling, party committees had not been able to take advantage of those same low rates. That distinction had traditionally benefited Democrats, whose candidates tend to raise more money than their committees. The opposite is true for Republicans.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

Republicans have pushed for ways to undo this advantage, notably in a Supreme Court case last term in which Republican groups successfully argued to lift coordinated spending limits between political parties and candidates.

In late June, in a 6-to-3 decision split along ideological lines, the justices sided with Republicans.

With a decision in their favor, Republicans had planned to coordinate with candidates to buy up TV ad time under the lower rates.

But four Democratic candidates from the battleground states of Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio brought a separate but related legal challenge to the lower ad rates.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina and Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan together challenged a notice by the Federal Communications Commission, the government agency that regulates broadcasters, that had alerted political parties and committees that they would now be entitled to the low rates.

On Aug. 25, a divided three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit sided with the Democratic challengers. Judge Robert B. King, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, wrote for the majority that the statute was “unambiguous” that only political candidates, not parties, are entitled to the low advertising rates. He added that the F.C.C. notice represented a “significant and unilateral expansion” of the rule.

In dissent, Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, an appointee of President Ronald Reagan, wrote that the appeals court’s decision represented “nothing less than an upending of settled campaign finance ground rules right in the middle of an election season.”

National Republican groups then filed an emergency application to the Supreme Court asking the justices to step in and clear the way for them to get the lower ad rates. The Republican challengers argued that the lower court judges had — “in the midst of election season” — rewritten “longstanding rules about preferential broadcast rates for political ads.”

Lawyers for the Trump administration joined them, asking the court to immediately overturn the lower court’s ruling. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserted that despite the Democratic candidates’ claims that the new F.C.C. guideline would harm them, the new notice in fact did not favor candidates of either party.

In response, lawyers for the Democratic candidates argued that the federal agency action meant they were “facing imminent, irreparable harm.”

Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting.

item.title: Former Staff Members Threaten to Expose Fetterman’s Internal Messages
item.description:
Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, has for years detested the day-to-day duties of his job, dismissing such tasks as going to hearings and casting votes as a “performative” waste of time.

Now, a group of his disillusioned former staff members — of which there are many — is threatening to reveal more about his private disdain for what is expected of him as an elected representative of 13 million constituents.

On Friday afternoon, a new account, @FettermanStaff, sprang up on X, threatening to publicize unflattering material about the first-term senator, including screen shots of his internal communications.

It came after The Wall Street Journal published fresh revelations highlighting Mr. Fetterman’s deep antipathy to the daily work of being a senator, including meeting with groups from his state and attending a funeral for fallen police officers.

“Why do I have to keep meeting with CHOP,” said a text message attributed to him that was published by The Wall Street Journal, but not independently verified by The New York Times, referring to the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

After an aide explained that its representatives were concerned about vaccines and Medicaid cuts, he responded, according to the Journal: “Well, I’m not. I’m convinced they just want free trips to DC.”

The new social media account, which two former staff members confirmed was authentic and described as a group effort, promised that communications like this were plentiful and would soon be on public display. The former aides spoke about the effort on the condition of anonymity.

Even in Washington, where political tell-all books are plentiful and staff leaks are common, such disclosures on a broad scale would be a remarkable breach of the confidentiality that almost always surrounds public officials’ communications with their aides, and a reflection of just how profoundly Mr. Fetterman has alienated people who once worked for him.

“We’re a group of former campaign & Senate staffers for John Fetterman who are disgusted with what he’s become,” the group wrote in its first post, calling the Journal’s report “the tip of the iceberg.”

“It’s even worse than you thought.”

The anonymous account said the people behind it planned to share stories that would “show Pennsylvanians exactly who their Senator is.” It said the first “drop” of information would land on Sept. 14, when the Senate is scheduled to return to session, but could be delayed for a day if Mr. Fetterman skips the Monday night votes, as he often does.

The social media post appeared designed to catch Mr. Fetterman's attention on a platform where he spends much of his time: The group follows just two accounts, his personal and official handles.

Mr. Fetterman did not respond to a text message seeking comment.

About 69 percent of likely Democratic voters in Pennsylvania view Mr. Fetterman negatively, according to a poll conducted last month by The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University. Most Republicans in his state, however, now hold a positive view of the Democrat who has become a fixture on conservative news outlets, bashing the policies of his own party.

All of that has driven speculation that Mr. Fetterman might leave the Democratic Party to become a Republican or an independent, a move he has vowed he will “never” make.

It has also energized Democrats in Pennsylvania to unseat Mr. Fetterman should he seek re-election in 2028. The progressive Working Families Party announced last year it would recruit and support a primary opponent to challenge him.

Mr. Fetterman, who was elected in 2022 as a self-proclaimed champion of working-class voters, had a life-threatening stroke in the middle of the most competitive Senate race in the country.

Shortly after being sworn in, he checked himself in to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to be treated for depression for six weeks, and appeared to make a remarkable recovery as he began speaking out about the importance of getting help when needed. But then in 2024, he began retreating from the job, rarely attending committee meetings, casting votes or holding town halls.

And as he has tacked right on the issue of Israel — he has said that if his party turns against Israel, it would be a “red line” that would prompt him to leave — and began picking fights with the left, his former aides have been increasingly outspoken about their disappointment in and aversion to the lawmaker he has become.

One former staff member, Tré Easton, reposted a message on Friday that described Mr. Fetterman as a “soulless ghoul.”

“Can confirm,” Mr. Easton, who said he was not associated with the new account, wrote online.

In another post, Mr. Easton wrote: “He’s an embarrassment to the commonwealth and fundamentally unfit for public office.”

item.title: Prosecutors Won’t Try to Reinstate Key 9/11 Confession Taken After Torture
item.description:
Military prosecutors have decided not to appeal to try to reinstate a key confession by Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11 attacks.

It was an apparent end to a yearslong effort by the government to defend statements obtained from him under brutal conditions in overseas C.I.A. prisons, and a bid to keep the trial for him and three others on track for the summer of 2028 at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba.

Prosecutors notified Sept. 11 victims and their family members of the decision on Friday, a week before the 25th anniversary of the attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania and the Pentagon. Many of the families have been deeply disappointed that it has taken so long to get the death-penalty trial started.

The U.S. government had long argued that the statements Mr. Mohammed made to F.B.I. agents at Guantánamo in 2007 were untainted by his isolation and harsh treatment in secret overseas C.I.A. prisons from 2003 to 2006. While held in the so-called black sites, he was subjected to 183 rounds of waterboarding.

But a military judge ruled last month that what Mr. Mohammed told the agents was involuntary, in part because he was not allowed to consult a lawyer and was not explicitly told that those particular interrogations could be used to prosecute him.

Danielle Reddan, the prosecution team’s liaison to victims in the Guantánamo cases, wrote the families in a short letter that “an appeal could jeopardize the hard-earned June 5, 2028, trial date.” Ms. Reddan, who is also a former Brooklyn prosecutor, added that appealing the judge’s ruling could result in Mr. Mohammed being tried separately from the other defendants in the case.

For more than a decade, prosecutors have sought to put on trial five men jointly in the conspiracy, as alleged plotters, trainers, recruiters and financiers, to spare the victims the pain of separate trials. But in 2023, a judge found Ramzi bin al-Shibh, an accused deputy in the hijacking plot, mentally incompetent and removed him from the case. Another judge is now handling his proceedings.

That leaves the three other defendants in different pretrial postures.

Two of the defendants, Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, are awaiting a ruling by the trial judge, Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, on whether their 2007 confessions at Guantánamo were voluntary and can be used against them.

Prosecutors have appealed to try to reinstate the 2007 confessions of the fourth defendant, Ammar al-Baluchi, who is Mr. Mohammed’s nephew. A judge suppressed Mr. Baluchi’s statement because of his prior torture by the C.I.A., and the circumstances of his confinement at Guantánamo.

Prosecutors had described those so-called clean team confessions as their best evidence in the death-penalty case. They sought a “Law & Order” moment with Frank Pellegrino, a retired F.B.I. agent who tracked Mr. Mohammed for years, describing for a military jury how he and Mr. Mohammed spent four days in January 2007 discussing the Sept. 11 plot.

But the prosecutors have other proposed evidence for the trial, including transcripts from secretly recorded discussions between prisoners in a recreation yard at Guantánamo; documents detailing money transfers; and, possibly, information from an interview Mr. Mohammed and Mr. bin al-Shibh gave to an Al Jazeera reporter before they were captured in Pakistan in 2002.

Mr. Mohammed’s will not be the first trial to proceed without the “clean team” confessions.

An Army judge previously threw out the F.B.I. interrogations of a Saudi man at Guantánamo, Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, who is accused of plotting Al Qaeda’s bombing of the U.S.S. Cole off Yemen. Prosecutors dropped an appeal, and selection of a military jury in the death-penalty trial of Mr. Nashiri is scheduled to start in October.

Legal experts noted that the decision not to appeal Colonel Schrama’s decision does not prevent prosecutors from going back to him directly and seeking reconsideration of his decision to suppress Mr. Mohammed’s confessions. They would have to find a serious legal error in the 45-page ruling, which has yet to be released, or invoke a change in the law.

item.title: F.B.I. Investigates Sale of Millions of Stolen Driver’s Licenses
item.description:
The F.B.I. is investigating the theft and sale of scans of millions of identity documents belonging to people in the United States and Canada.

The documents were being promoted on a database called Nexus, which advertised on a dark corner of the internet this week as including about 170 million identity documents in all.

The availability of the documents was reported on Tuesday by Krebs on Security, a blog run by Brian Krebs, a former Washington Post reporter with an expertise in cybersecurity.

The F.B.I. declined to provide details about the origins of the breach, citing an open investigation. But in an emailed statement, it confirmed “that it is looking into the incident.”

The breach, which is said to include digital copies of driver’s licenses, travel documents and medical cards, is part of an increasingly common pattern of scams and frauds in which stolen materials can be used to create fake identity documents, said James E. Lee, the president of the Identity Theft Resource Center, a nonprofit that tracks breaches and advises victims.

The addition of photographs in this particular theft can make it easier to create fake credentials.

“Unfortunately, the size of this breach is no longer uncommon, but the nature of the data that has been compromised makes it a particularly risky breach,” Mr. Lee said.

Nexus first promoted the sale of the stolen scanned identity documents on a Russian cybercrime site called Exploit, Mr. Krebs reported.

Previews of the site’s offerings, some accompanied by photographs, included a driver’s license belonging to Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, Mr. Krebs reported.

“The department is aware of these reports and is evaluating them,” the Defense Department said in an emailed statement.

Infoblox, a network security company that maintains a database derived from its access to dark web forums, provided a statement by email on Friday that quoted Nexus’s advertisement in which it first offered the millions of documents for purchase.

The Nexus advertisement said that, in addition to 160 million records of North American driver’s licenses and identification cards, it was also offering for sale more than 10 million international identity documents, travel documents, residency cards and medical cards.

It said about 500,000 documents were being added every day.

“We are offering access to our proprietary and exclusive database of breached identity documents,” the advertisement said.

Nexus added that it had “persistent access to a major identity verification company and its customers,” including “multiple Fortune 500 companies.”

“We have been continuously exfiltrating new data for over a year into our private database,” the advertisement said.

Zach Edwards, a researcher with Infoblox Threat Intel, said in the statement that the breach was remarkable because of its size and the access it gained over such a long period.

“This attack would have been shocking if the threat actors merely stole a database with over 150+ million driver’s licenses and other credentials,” he said. “But the fact that this was also allegedly a real-time ongoing breach with new credentials being submitted to the vendor and stolen by the threat actors, and that these credentials were being submitted from countless enterprise providers, means that this attack created legitimate national security risks for high-profile individuals.”

Mr. Edwards said in an interview that, because of the enormous scope of the breach, and because not all of the stolen documents have addresses, notifying victims would be a challenge.

Krebs on Security said that, after it published its report on Tuesday, the Nexus identity theft service vanished from the dark web, referring to parts of the internet that are not searchable and that are often used for criminal activity.

Mr. Lee of the Identity Theft Resource Center encouraged Americans and Canadians to be vigilant in response to the theft.

“There’s still a lot we don’t know about the data and the source, but people should be on the lookout for signs their identities are being misused and an increase in highly personalized phishing attacks,” he said.

item.title: Judge Orders Trump Officials to Divulge Names of Those Who Set Up $1.8 Billion Fund
item.description:
A federal magistrate judge ordered the Trump administration on Friday to reveal the identities of the people who devised a contentious plan to create a $1.8 billion fund to compensate those who believed they were wronged by political prosecutions.

The order by the magistrate judge, Ivan D. Davis, could shed further light on how the fund was put together. The plan to create the fund, which could have funneled taxpayer money to the president’s allies, drew repeated scrutiny. It prompted a rare rebuke from Senate Republicans, and imperiled the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general.

Mr. Blanche has repeatedly said the fund is dead, but President Trump has been more circumspect, indicating his support for compensating people like the rioters who were prosecuted for attacking the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

Judge Davis’s order, issued in Federal District Court in Alexandria, Va., came as part of a lawsuit challenging the legality of the fund and another measure by the Justice Department that benefited Mr. Trump. That provision granted the president, his family and his businesses expansive protections against all past tax investigations.

Both the fund and the tax immunity deal emerged from backroom negotiations between Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers and senior Justice Department officials. The measures were made public after Mr. Trump agreed to dismiss a lawsuit he had filed against the Internal Revenue Service, seeking damages for claims that the agency had failed to stop the release of some of his tax returns to news organizations.

A federal judge in Florida later excoriated both the suit and the way in which it was dismissed. She said that the suit was an improper exercise in self-dealing because the president had brought claims against a federal agency that he himself controlled. She also asserted that the dismissal had been worked out with the intent to evade judicial oversight.

The suit seeking to kill the fund and the tax immunity deal was brought in Virginia by a group of plaintiffs that includes a former federal prosecutor who was fired by the Trump administration after working on Jan. 6-related cases. The group has claimed that the program was unfairly designed to help only supporters of the president.

The union representing I.R.S. workers later joined the suit, claiming that the tax provisions were illegal and could put its employees in the untenable position of carrying out unlawful orders.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs hailed the decision.

“Today’s order granting discovery is a significant step in getting to the bottom of the slush fund,” said Aman George, a lawyer for Democracy Forward, which filed the suit.

The Justice Department did not immediately comment on the ruling.

item.title: Where Will Lindsay Clancy Go Now?
item.description:
Lindsay Clancy will return to Tewksbury Hospital, a state-run psychiatric facility where she has been held during trial, her lawyer said, after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial on Friday in the murder case against her.

Ms. Clancy’s symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the months before she killed her three children were at the center of her defense. Had she been acquitted, she most certainly would have continued to be hospitalized.

Experts say she may have been sent to a high-security forensic psychiatric hospital — a center to treat people who have stood criminal trial — for long-term mental health care.

Several psychiatrists said that for many women, symptoms of postpartum psychosis are treated and resolved within a year. But regardless of the ultimate outcome of her case, Ms. Clancy will most likely be treated for other ongoing issues, such as suicidal thoughts and a potential diagnosis of bipolar disorder, which can be a risk factor for postpartum psychosis.

Patients often work with a team of psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, nurses, peer advisers and other therapists while they’re hospitalized, said Dr. Susan Hatters-Friedman, a forensic and reproductive psychiatrist at Case Western Reserve University and the former president of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law.

The goal of forensic hospitalization is not just to manage patients’ mental illness, but also to prepare them to heal and possibly return to society.

The treatment plan for patients like Ms. Clancy might include helping them cope with the killings of their children.

“Many of these women have no significant past psychiatric history, and then get very ill very quickly,” said Dr. Nicole H. Cirino, a psychiatrist who serves on the Postpartum Psychosis Task Force at Postpartum Support International, a nonprofit.

She continued: “Reconciling that and thinking about how to move forward, particularly if they have legal involvement, is really something that is quite complicated and takes some time.”

In many states, including Massachusetts, where Ms. Clancy was prosecuted, people who are found not guilty by reason of insanity often spend more time hospitalized than they would have in prison, said Dr. Renée Sorrentino, a forensic psychiatrist who is licensed in Massachusetts.

In Massachusetts, she said, Ms. Clancy would be reviewed for discharge on an annual basis. Doctors could recommend that she be discharged from the hospital if they believed that her symptoms had improved and if they determined that she was not a danger to others.

The Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office would then be notified. If it disagreed with the medical team’s assessment, it could obtain its own experts or argue in court that Ms. Clancy should remain hospitalized. A judge would then decide whether she could be released, Dr. Sorrentino said.

“Humane mental health treatment is really important for her, and for us to think about as a society,” said Dr. Nirmaljit Dhami, the medical director of an inpatient psychiatric ward in California focused on perinatal mental health and preventive care.

In 2012, Deanna Laney, a Texas woman who was found not guilty by reason of insanity for killing two of her children and seriously injuring a third, was released from a psychiatric hospital after treatment. Several conditions were placed on her release.

Some women, however, like Andrea Yates, a Texas woman who in 2006 was found not guilty by reason of insanity in the killings of her five children, choose to waive their right to a review and remain hospitalized instead.

If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for a list of additional resources.

item.title: Fake Version of Republican Midterm Convention Website Redirects to Epstein Files
item.description:
Someone is very intent on making sure voters don’t forget about the Epstein files.

Republicans eager to find out more about the party’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Dallas next week got a surprise this week: a website that initially purported to be the Republican National Committee’s official convention page but then redirected to the Justice Department’s library of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender.

It wasn’t a hack. The real convention site, at gopconvention.com, remains operational, prominently featuring an outline of Texas and this bold claim: “The Golden Age of America Has Just Begun.”

Some users searching for the site on Google, however, were directed to an impostor website — at gopdallas2026.com — that earned a spot much higher in search results than the real site.

Google’s preview of the fake page promises “details about the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, Sept. 9-10 including registration, VIP experiences.”

It does not deliver anything of the sort. Instead, a click on the site takes the user to “justice.gov/epstein,” something of a headache for Republicans and President Trump, whose ties to Mr. Epstein have angered the MAGA base and served as an ongoing irritant in an election year expected to be a referendum on his presidency.

The R.N.C. said it believed a creative agency with Democratic ties was behind the fake site, pointing to a Daily Mail article published Friday that cited a Republican opposition research firm’s digital forensic analysis.

“Democrats are too broke to have their own midterm convention, so they settled for a sad, fake little website,” Zach Parkinson, a spokesman for the R.N.C., said in a statement.

Data from an internet registration database, ICANN, showed that the domain was registered on July 7 and updated on Sept. 3. An archived version of the fake site shows that it appeared for weeks as a more straight-ahead impostor of the actual Republican convention site, leading with fireworks, a photo of Mr. Trump and the title “The Great American Comeback Midterm Convention.” It even included a list of potential speakers, such as Mr. Trump and various cabinet secretaries.

The Daily Mail article said that when a reporter reached out to the founder of the Democratic agency, Yosi Sargent, on Thursday, the fake site switched to the Epstein files redirect.

On Friday evening, Mr. Sargent appeared to acknowledge he was behind the site in a text message to The New York Times.

“We made you look,” he wrote. “Satire is such an important art form to draw attention to important issues, like the Epstein files.”

The spoof tricked people for weeks, with news outlets initially citing information it presented and some reporters filing for credentials on the fake website.

“If you were a reporter who submitted a request for credentials through this website and are now left stranded, you now know who screwed you over,” Mr. Parkinson said.

The fake site did include a disclaimer: “This website is an independent informational resource and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by the Republican National Committee (RNC), the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention, the American Airlines Center, or any official convention entity.”

As recently as Aug. 27, gopdallas2026.com still showed the duplicate site and was not linking to the Epstein files. Nearly 140 other websites linked to it, including The Dallas Morning News, the conservative Daily Wire news site and the New Jersey Federation of Republican Women.

At some point after that date, the site began redirecting to the Epstein files.

Kate Conger contributed reporting.

item.title: What to Know About Trump’s Efforts to Block Voting by Mail
item.description:
We are less than two months from Election Day and President Trump is still trying to block millions of Americans from receiving ballots in the mail.

The president’s allies at the U.S. Postal Service are seeking to implement a new rule that places a host of requirements on states that allow mail voting that would be nearly impossible for them to meet this close to an election.

The effort is part of Trump’s yearslong endeavor to restrict access to voting and cast doubts on American elections, which has not abated since he lost the 2020 presidential election and disputed the results.

The story is complicated, hard to follow and subject to change at any moment at the hands of federal judges. There are different court challenges and standard legal arguments about who has standing to sue and when they can do it. To help understand where things are, I consulted with my Times colleagues who cover voting, the Supreme Court, the Postal Service and the legal cases: Nick Corasaniti, Abbie VanSickle, Zach Montague and Eileen Sullivan.

Below are answers to five big questions about mail voting and how Trump’s proposals will affect the ballots that may or may not come to your home in the weeks ahead.

Trump administration officials want to severely curtail the use of ballots sent to voters by mail.

A rule published by the Postal Service would require all states to upload lists of voters who receive mail ballots to a governmental portal. That portal is not yet online, and it is unclear if courts will block the rule or even if the portal will work.

(A previous federal government portal, former President Barack Obama’s healthcare.gov, had a far longer runway before it launched and was a catastrophic failure.)

The rule also requires any state sending ballots by mail to use a special bar code on the envelopes. Those bar codes would in many cases require the counties and municipalities that administer elections to acquire dedicated printers that they do not already have. Doing this in the weeks remaining before state laws require mail ballots to be sent would likely be an insurmountable task for thousands of local elections officials.

Some of them are already have. There is nothing yet stopping other states from sending theirs too.

North Carolina and Delaware began mailing ballots Friday. Sixteen more states are scheduled to send ballots within the next two weeks.

We do not know yet whether the Postal Service, under the direction of Trump appointees, will continue to process ballots without delay if jurisdictions do not abide by the new rules.

The worst-case scenario: Voters would have to return ballots in person to a drop box or a local elections office, rather than mailing them back.

Lots of voters do this already. In 2024, about 21 percent of mail ballots were returned in drop boxes or to a local clerk, according to the MIT Elections and Data Lab.

But this is not always possible. College students, workers on a long-term assignment far from home or snowbirds who split time between warm and cold weather climates would all be far from communities in which they vote.

Mail voting is so prevalent now that many states have built their entire voting infrastructure around it.

Washington State, one of a handful that mails ballots to every registered voter, no longer has traditional in-person polling places. Arizona’s secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, told me recently that his state counts on 80 percent of its voters casting ballots they receive in the mail and is not equipped for millions of people to suddenly vote in person.

Some elections officials in mail-heavy states are considering creating pop-up voting centers to handle massive numbers of people if mail balloting is disrupted.

Others may ask voters to pick up their ballots at elections offices or municipal buildings. Real discussions are taking place among some Democratic elections officials about creating a system to have voters cast ballots online.

Several groups are trying to stop this effort in the courts. Democratic attorneys general and voting rights organizations have sued to block the Postal Service from implementing its new rules.

The Constitution grants states and Congress responsibility for elections, not the executive branch. Groups challenging the new rule argue that the Postal Service, a constitutionally mandated executive branch agency, has overstepped its bounds. The Trump administration says the agency is acting under federal law.

As of right now — Friday afternoon — a federal judge in Boston is weighing whether to keep in place a block on the Postal Service rules. Whatever she decides, the case is certain to be appealed, though the Trump administration is likely to ask the Supreme Court to rule on the case before a critical mass of states distributes mail ballots.

quote of the day

That was Gloria Steinem on “Real Time With Bill Maher” in February 2016, reflecting on why she believed Senator Bernie Sanders had outsize support from young voters, including women, during his presidential campaign.

It was, in retrospect, a weird time, 10 years and forever ago, Michael Kruse writes.

One Number

That’s how many voters in North Carolina have requested absentee ballots for the general election.

On Friday, North Carolina became the first state to forge ahead with its standard vote-by-mail program as the Trump administration escalates its efforts to restrict the practice.

item.title: In Complex Cases, Consensus Can Be Hard to Reach
item.description:
As Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial came to an end on Friday, there was no shortage of drama.

The courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., was thronged with observers. Ms. Clancy’s lawyer butted heads with the judge and made a doomed appeal to prevent the declaration of a mistrial. Audience members gasped.

But the most pivotal decision took place behind closed doors. After spending nearly 40 hours in deliberation — and half of those in deadlock — jurors said they could not come to a unanimous verdict on whether Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible for strangling her three children in 2023. A single juror was said to be at odds with everyone else in the room.

It was a remarkable outcome, said Valerie Hans, a Cornell law professor who studies jury behavior. “Hung juries are not frequent,” she added. “Maybe one out of every 20 cases in criminal courts results in a hung jury.”

Jury verdicts in serious criminal cases across the United States must be unanimous, a rule that was affirmed in a 2020 Supreme Court decision interpreting the Sixth Amendment of the Constitution.

“It’s entirely an artifact of history and tradition,” said Christopher Slobogin, a law professor at Vanderbilt University. He added that the standards for criminal cases were high because a guilty verdict could result in a deprivation of liberty.

Dr. Hans says that failures of consensus are most likely in cases where the evidence is close — that is, not clearly favoring either side — and complex.

The Clancy trial seemed to fit those parameters. Jurors sat through four weeks of emotional, often harrowing, testimony. They watched expert witnesses reach opposite conclusions on Ms. Clancy’s criminal culpability in the death of her children. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued for an insanity defense, claiming that she had been in the throes of postpartum psychosis.

The jurors, nine women and three men, wore increasingly grim expressions as their deadlock dragged on, even after the judge, William Sullivan, delivered a set of instructions on Wednesday known as the “dynamite charge” in a last-ditch effort to nudge them toward a verdict.

Professor Slobogin said it was notable that Judge Sullivan’s efforts had failed. “Typically, if there is a hung jury, the judge is able to convince the jury to go back and reach a unanimous verdict,” he said.

But on Friday, the jurors said in a note to the court that “with a heavy heart,” they had been unable to reach a consensus.

According to Dr. Hans, the jurors probably took their work very seriously. “People can be very flippant outside the jury context,” she said, “and yet there’s something about getting sworn in as a juror that is sobering.”

That extends beyond the courthouse, she added: Research suggests that people who serve on juries tend to become more civically engaged after the trial ends.

For now, the jurors’ work at the Plymouth courthouse is done. Ms. Clancy still faces murder charges, and prosecutors will decide whether to try their case all over again.

If they do, a brand-new jury will be sworn in.

item.title: Tetris Owner Denounces Trump White House Clone of Game
item.description:
The Tetris Company, the company that owns the rights to the classic video game, denounced a clone of the game produced by the Trump administration that has the player block space aliens and zombies from crossing the U.S.-Mexican border.

It was the latest incident in which an owner of a creative work objected to the Trump administration’s use of it.

Build the Wall, the White House version of Tetris, urges the player to “protect the border from the incoming horde,” which is rhetoric that President Trump and members of his administration often use about immigrants.

“The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall,’” the company said in a statement on social media, adding that “at Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them. To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we’re grateful to have you in our community.”

On Thursday, the White House shared a page on its official government website that featured five simple video games that promoted Trump administration policies. They are clones of existing games, and the Tetris clone is called Build the Wall with the subtitle Zombie Border Siege. Another game called Rio Run is a clone of the Snake game, where players catch and imprison an increasingly long line of immigrants on the southern border.

Tetris is a puzzle game. Blocks of different shapes fall down the screen and must be sorted into complete lines as they fill up the screen, gradually accelerating. The game was created by Alexey Pajitnov, a Soviet software engineer, in 1984. The Tetris Company continues to license many variants of the game, some of which are marketed to children with Nintendo cartoon characters like Mario, Kirby and Donkey Kong.

Build the Wall has those blocks take the form of the southern border wall, physically blocking aliens and zombies that explode when they collide with the wall.

In its statement, the Tetris Company added, “P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously.”

The Tetris Company won a significant copyright case in 2012 against a company that made a Tetris clone, a ruling that reinforced that the owner of a video game could protect the “look and feel” of the game under copyright law.

A social media video accompanying the White House games also invoked Sega, the creators of Sonic the Hedgehog. The intro to the video includes an image mimicking the company’s logo, a recording of the company’s name being sung and a copyrighted song from the Sonic games.

A long list of musicians have denounced Mr. Trump using their music at his rallies, and some have taken legal action to protect their copyrighted material. In November, the musician Olivia Rodrigo, who is Filipino American, condemned the use of her music in a post by the Department of Homeland Security promoting the Trump administration’s mass deportation effort, writing underneath the post: “don’t ever use my songs to promote your racist, hateful propaganda.”

Trump administration social media posts have sometimes sought to appeal specifically to gamers, especially young men who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024.

One noteworthy post in October by the Department of Homeland Security equated immigrants to the flesh-eating aliens known as “the Flood” in the Halo video game series. The post, which featured an image from the game of a machine-gun armed vehicle, included the caption: “destroy the Flood” with a link to the recruiting website for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Microsoft, which owns Halo, said in a statement at the time that the company “does not have anything to share on this matter.”

item.title: ‘This Is My Money’: Trump Says He Will Spend Some of His War Chest on Republicans
item.description:
President Trump said Friday he plans to spend “probably” $400 million to $500 million on midterm election races, but added that he also intends to hold back resources as Republicans openly beg him to stop sitting on his money and give them financial support.

“This is my money that I control,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House. At the same time, he said he believes Republicans can do well in November and he will help.

“I’m going to spend whatever amount of money is necessary,” he said.

As his party struggles to maintain control of Congress, Mr. Trump has been criticized from within his own party as tightfisted.

The president told reporters he estimated he has “like close to a billion dollars” to spend on politics, a total that perhaps includes Republican National Committee funds and money in Mr. Trump’s campaign account. Federal Election Commission documents show that MAGA Inc., Mr. Trump’s political action committee, has about $403 million on hand.

This year, Mr. Trump has spent money to help another candidate once, boosting Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina through last month’s Republican primary in what most political observers view as a safe state for Republicans.

The G.O.P. is at risk of losing the House and, to a lesser degree, the Senate, dragged down by Mr. Trump’s low approval ratings. While some candidates have attempted to distance themselves from the president, most are still hoping that Mr. Trump will come through with financial support for their races.

“I’m going to be making contributions to various campaigns of people that I think are good, Republicans that I think are good,” he said.

Even so, Mr. Trump said he planned to save some of his funds for races that are still two years off.

“I expect to have money left over, and we can use that for ’28,” he said.
