item.title: Judge Once Again Blocks Mail-In Ballot Rules
item.description:
A federal judge in Boston ruled for the third time on Friday that the Trump administration’s plans to restrict mail-in voting are likely unconstitutional and it should be prevented from implementing them ahead of the midterm election.

Judge Indira Talwani had already temporarily blocked the U.S. Postal Service from moving forward, in a ruling that was set to expire Sept. 10. The new order extends that block indefinitely.

She wrote that the Trump administration appeared to be denying that its effort at the Postal Service was “an election rule” to get around that the Constitution reserves the power to administer elections to the states and Congress.

“This denial rings hollow,” she wrote. “The final rule explicitly and exclusively regulates election mail.”

What the ruling did not do was move the issue much closer to a resolution, even with time rapidly running out for state election officials to start distributing mail-in ballots to voters. The Trump administration had already appealed her temporary block to the Supreme Court, and the justices are likely to have the final word on President Trump’s plans ahead of the election.

The Trump administration filed an appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit less than two hours later.

The ruling came just a day after Judge Talwani held a two-hour hearing in Boston, with lawyers representing large coalitions of Democratic-led states and voting rights groups squared off with lawyers representing the Postal Service and a smaller group of Republican-led states that support the rule.

Judge Talwani reviewed their concerns about the Postal Service rule, which would require states to report to the Postal Service which of their voters are qualified to use mail-in ballots, and to adopt a new ballot envelope designed to be scanned and linked to voters. The Postal Service could withhold mail delivery of ballots in states that don’t comply.

She said she believed the concerns among states and election officials that it was too late to adopt the changes without widespread mishaps and delays. The election is now only 60 days away.

Judge Talwani wrote the rule appeared to force states to work against their own privacy laws and imposed requirements that appeared certain to result in some voters being disqualified.

“Having considered this series of hurdles for officials against the backdrop of an impending election, and mindful of the fact that any minor malfunction will result in the denial of mail ballots, the court concludes that disenfranchisement for plaintiff organizations’ members, regardless of residence, is practically inevitable,” Judge Talwani wrote.

In particular, Judge Talwani questioned why the Postal Service was moving ahead with exceptional urgency to get the rule approved in time for the midterms while also insisting it was a relatively routine action that required only minor clerical changes. She also cast doubt on Mr. Trump’s claims that the rule was necessary for election security.

She wrote that proceeding so soon before the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.”

“And, on the other side,” she wrote, she found that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”

Several officials from Democratic-led states welcomed the ruling.

“We are glad that this court has stopped the Postal Service from impacting who can receive a ballot in the 2026 election,” Jena Griswold, Colorado’s secretary of state, said in a statement. “The Postal Service must stick to its job of delivering the mail, rather than trying to decide who gets to vote.”

Still, Judge Talwani wrote that she would not second guess or seek to prevent any of a number of Republican-led states that support the rule from meeting its requirements voluntarily. She also said the decision on Friday addressed only the implementation of the rule for the current election cycle, and that courts could later sort out whether it was lawful in its entirety.

Like in her two previous rulings, she wrote that the rule appeared to exceed the Postal Service’s statutory authority by assigning broad authority to the service to regulate election mail, beyond what lawmakers intended. She added that with each passing week, it had become increasingly unrealistic to expect states to be able to comply.

Jeff Jackson, the North Carolina attorney general, said in a statement that the administration’s request to the Supreme Court on Thursday came just as the state was scheduled to send out ballots to voters on Friday.

“That would throw our election into chaos,” Mr. Jackson said. “The ballots are printed, the process is underway, and North Carolinians deserve a lawful and orderly election.”

The decision on Friday technically appeared to render the Trump administration’s appeals of Judge Talwani’s previous orders moot.

But at the hearing on Thursday, Michael Velchik, a Justice Department attorney representing the Postal Service, indicated that if she took this step, the Trump administration would likely return to the Supreme Court to “start the process again.”

Nicholas Corasaniti contributed reporting.

item.title: C.D.C. Says No Deaths This Year Attributed to Measles
item.description:
Escalating a political fight over two deaths in Pennsylvania, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Friday that it did not have any records to indicate “measles is the underlying cause” of any deaths in the country this year.

The phrasing on its website, part of the agency’s weekly update to measles tallies, is the latest development in a heated disagreement between state and federal officials over whether the two deaths were a result of measles or merely coincided with the infection. The dispute echoes similar quarrels over causes of death during the coronavirus pandemic.

The C.D.C.’s update came even as the coroner for Lancaster County, where the deaths reportedly occurred, announced on Friday that a 6-week-old child in the county had died from measles. The child, who died last month, had a rare genetic disorder called Amish microcephaly, according to the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

The Department of Health and Human Services directed a request for comment to a social media post by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“The facts emerging now demonstrate why C.D.C. waited for the evidence rather than allowing political grandstanding to dictate its reporting,” Mr. Kennedy said in the post.

Infants with Amish microcephaly typically live only about six months, and the infant in question died at approximately 2 months old, the secretary said.

Pennsylvania has been at the center of a rapidly escalating measles outbreak. Nearly 600 people have contracted the disease in the state, and nearly 100 have been hospitalized. Nationwide, the number of measles cases this year has topped 3,000, the highest in 35 years.

Last week, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a Democrat, announced the two deaths in his state and said the federal government was partly to blame for hesitancy surrounding measles vaccinations. The following day, Mr. Kennedy accused the governor of taking “giddy delight” in announcing the deaths and suggested the reports might have been “fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers.”

In its measles update last week, the C.D.C. added an asterisked statement that the “available information does not establish” whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths in Pennsylvania and that the agency needed to review further information.

The New York Times reported on Monday that the C.D.C.’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, had ordered agency officials to challenge Pennsylvania’s reporting of the two deaths, shunning the agency’s normal procedure of accepting data shared by states and amplifying the comments by Mr. Kennedy, who is her boss.

The C.D.C.’s update this week retains the asterisk under the death tally but makes no reference to Pennsylvania’s reports. The agency instead says that its National Center for Health Statistics “does not currently have any death records” indicating measles as a cause of death and that it will update its numbers as more information becomes available.

item.title: Trump’s Latest Clemency Grants Benefit Drug Offenders, Union Boss
item.description:
President Trump issued 30 clemency grants on Thursday, including to a drug dealer-turned-business executive, a longtime Philadelphia union boss convicted of bribery and a former Navy sailor imprisoned for firearms offenses.

The clemency grants were confirmed by White House officials and representatives for the recipients.

They went to an eclectic group, continuing Mr. Trump’s unpredictable and unorthodox use of pardons that wipe away most consequences of convictions and commutations, which cut short sentences.

While other presidents have drawn criticism for using clemency to reward supporters or protect allies, Mr. Trump has taken it to a new level. His use of clemency has spawned a cottage industry of lawyers and lobbyists offering to use their connections to bring cases to his attention in exchange for hefty fees.

Thursday’s beneficiaries included some prominent figures. But the pardons also encompassed lower-profile people who were facing long sentences and lacked obvious connections to the president or his allies.

Among them was Holly Leanne Frantzen, who had served more than a decade of a nearly 17-year sentence for drug charges. The White House did not indicate whether she had received a pardon or a commutation.

In a statement pleading for clemency on the website of a prisoners’ rights group, Ms. Frantzen admitted to past struggles with drug addiction. But she indicated that she was working on completing an apprenticeship in plumbing, and that her rehabilitation behind bars had “compelled me to believe that there is hope.”

Alice Marie Johnson, the White House pardon czar, who has focused on elevating the cases of women and nonviolent drug offenders, highlighted Ms. Frantzen in a statement Friday announcing the clemency grants.

“My prayer is that each of these 30 people makes the most of this extraordinary second chance and becomes a greater blessing to their families, communities and the world,” Ms. Johnson said in a post on social media.

Mr. Trump also pardoned Emory Clash Jones, who served more than a decade in prison for a conviction related to selling crack cocaine.

A longtime associate of the rapper Jay-Z’s, Mr. Jones has been out of prison since 2010, according to Bureau of Prisons records. He has worked as an executive at Roc Nation, Jay-Z’s sprawling company.

In her statement, Ms. Johnson praised Mr. Jones as “an entrepreneur and creative leader whose journey reminds us how much people can grow — and how much good they can still do.”

In a letter to the judge overseeing the case in 2009, Jay-Z, writing under his given name Shawn Carter, indicated that he had known Mr. Jones for 15 years, and urged his release, praising his “intelligence, interpersonal skills and solid work ethic.”

Mr. Jones and Roc Nation did not respond to requests for comment.

Another clemency grant went to John Dougherty, who led a Philadelphia-based unit of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers for nearly three decades until he resigned in 2021 after he was convicted of bribing a City Council member there.

Mr. Dougherty, who is known as “Johnny Doc” and had exerted outsized influence in Philadelphia politics for decades, had served less than two years of a six-year prison sentence. The remainder of the sentence was wiped away by a commutation issued by Mr. Trump.

A White House official, who requested anonymity to discuss the president’s clemency decisions, said that Mr. Dougherty’s sentence was commuted to allow him to care for his terminally ill wife. Her father had been caring for her, but he passed away while Mr. Dougherty was in prison, the official said.

George Bochetto, a lawyer for Mr. Dougherty, said in an email on Friday that his client had been released from prison and was headed to Philadelphia “to be by his wife’s side.”

A pardon was granted to Patrick Adamiak, a former sailor who was sentenced in 2023 to 20 years in prison for possessing and selling illegal firearms from his home in Virginia.

The case of Mr. Adamiak, who goes by “Tate,” was championed by gun rights backers who supported Mr. Trump. They argued that his conviction was the result of unclear regulations and a frame job by a confidential informant.

Adam Kraut, the executive director of the Second Amendment Foundation, said in a statement that the case was “every gun owner’s worst nightmare.” Mr. Kraut added that “while Tate shouldn’t have endured what happened to him in the first place, we are thrilled he has finally received the pardon he deserves.”

item.title: North Carolina Adds New Restrictions to Vote-by-Mail Program
item.description:
The North Carolina State Board of Elections added new restrictions to its vote-by-mail program on Friday morning, making it easier for local election officials across the state to discard ballots.

Just hours after counties in the state began sending the nation’s first batch of mail ballots for the fall election, the five-member state board, which is controlled by Republicans, split on party lines to approve the changes. The new rule requires officials to disqualify ballots with an unsealed envelope and limits who can drop off mail ballots on behalf of another voter.

The changes are almost certain to cause some votes to be tossed. They come at a time when President Trump and his allies have repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread fraud in mail voting, and used those false claims to justify strict new voting policies.

On Friday, the three Republican board members sought to cast the changes as both procedural and necessary to ensure the integrity of state elections, echoing Mr. Trump’s arguments.

“It’s a ballot security issue to make sure the voter’s will and intent is being followed through,” Stacy “Four” Eggers, a Republican member of the board, said at the virtual meeting on Friday.

In part because of such claims, Democrats in recent years have voted by mail in higher numbers than Republicans, meaning that restrictions to mail voting are more likely to disenfranchise Democrats than Republicans. Mr. Trump has stated publicly that he believes restricting the practice would benefit his party in the fall midterms.

In North Carolina, roughly 5 percent of voters cast their ballots by mail in the 2024 presidential election, a far lower rate than many other states. But with a Senate race that could help determine which party controls the chamber, small margins could make the difference.

As of Friday afternoon, election officials in the state had shipped more than 47,000 absentee ballots, according to Jason Tyson, a spokesman for the state elections board. More than 42 percent of voters who requested the ballots were registered Democrats, according to preliminary data provided by Mr. Tyson. About 38 percent of the voters were unaffiliated; more than 18 percent were Republicans.

Democrats in the state, including those on the board of elections, argued that the changes sow confusion and could disenfranchise voters with disabilities or without internet access. They also criticized the Republicans for pushing through a new rule just nine weeks ahead of Election Day.

“North Carolina voters deserve transparency in their elections, not last-minute workarounds that could keep their vote from counting,” said Governor Josh Stein, a Democrat, in a statement. “I will continue to stand up for voters’ access to the ballot box.”

One of the Democratic members of the board, Jeff Carmon, appeared at the Friday meeting with a virtual background that depicted John Lewis, the late civil rights leader. The other, Siobhan Millen, criticized her Republican counterparts for characterizing the new rules as simply technical changes.

“This does affect the voter,” she said. “It affects whether your ballot counts. That’s huge. So an effort to say this is just a process thing, I think is incorrect.”

The new rules specify that in most cases, only a voter’s “near relative” or legal guardian can deliver their mail-in ballot in person on their behalf. If election officials find that the envelope is not adequately sealed and the voter is not present to do so, the rule requires county board staff to discard the ballot and issue a new one.

The board had voted earlier this summer to approve a broader array of changes that would have made it easier to discard certain ballots. But enough state residents filed written objections to trigger a process under state law that gives the final say to the state legislature.

The board’s action on Friday amounted to an administrative directive, which is a workaround allowing changes to election practices even as a more formal and expanded version of the rules has stalled in the General Assembly.

item.title: Postal Service Internal Watchdog Opens Inquiry After Whistle-Blower’s Complaint
item.description:
The U.S. Postal Service’s internal watchdog is opening an investigation into concerns raised in a whistle-blower report about the agency’s hasty effort to build a complex online system with voter data ahead of the midterm elections.

The online portal is intended to be an additional layer of screening for mail voting that President Trump called for in a March executive order. A whistle-blower said the system designed by the Postal Service had not gone through rigorous testing and could lead to substantial delays in voters’ receiving mail ballots.

Tara Linne, a spokeswoman for the Postal Service’s inspector general, said the office had received the whistle-blower report.

“We are currently analyzing the information and plan to conduct an independent review of these allegations,” Ms. Linne said in a statement Friday afternoon.

The executive order is facing several legal challenges, and its implementation has been indefinitely paused.

Most recently, the Postal Service said this voter data portal — an online system for states to upload information about voters receiving mail ballots — would be ready for use next week on a voluntary basis.

In a statement on Friday, the postmaster general, David P. Steiner, acknowledged the whistle-blower’s concerns about the pace of the project.

“Although development proceeded on an accelerated schedule, our standards for quality, security, and system integrity were not compromised,” Mr. Steiner said. “Testing and validation have been continuous throughout the development life cycle, and our process requires that deployment be delayed whenever significant defects or security vulnerabilities are identified, until those issues are appropriately resolved.”

Mr. Steiner said the additional screening of mail ballots was a necessary security measure to “facilitate enforcement of federal law and address concerns about election integrity.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread mail-in voting fraud, even as he voted by mail in two elections this year.

item.title: Judge Will Not Block Pentagon Move to Fire Stars and Stripes Journalists
item.description:
A federal judge in Washington will not immediately block the Pentagon’s move to fire three journalists at the federally funded but independent military news organization Stars and Stripes.

The ruling is an opening victory for the Pentagon’s efforts to exert control over the newspaper, which started publishing during the Civil War and has a long history of independent reporting.

Erik A. Slavin, the paper’s editor in chief; Lara S. Korte, its Middle East correspondent; and Max D. Lederer Jr., the paper’s publisher, accused the government of violating their First Amendment right to free speech. They asked the court to reject their terminations as well as new Pentagon policies that they say severely limit the editorial independence of their work.

The journalists also said their firings were related to their coverage of the worsening conditions on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, a Navy aircraft carrier that had been deployed to the Middle East for over nine months.

In July, CBS News interviewed Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte for a news segment on accusations of editorial interference at Stars and Stripes. Mr. Lederer, who had given Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte permission for the CBS interview, refused to fire them despite the Pentagon’s urging. Amid continued pressure, Mr. Lederer announced that he would soon retire and issued public statements on his strife with the Defense Department’s leadership. He was then served a termination notice.

In a hearing on Friday morning, Taryn Wilgus Null, a lawyer with Democracy Defenders Fund representing the Stars and Stripes employees, argued that her clients were speaking as “private citizens about a matter of public concern,” and therefore, their comments deserved the full protection of the First Amendment.

In a 24-page ruling, Judge Trevor N. McFadden of the Federal District Court in Washington reasoned that the public remarks by Mr. Slavin, Ms. Korte and Mr. Lederer “suggest that they spoke as part of their official duties and not as private citizens.” “They are thus unlikely to succeed on the merits of their First Amendment claim,” he wrote.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

Judge McFadden also rejected arguments that the journalists’ firings would cause a broader chilling effect among federal workers and federally funded news organizations, writing that “public employees are (or should be) aware that they are not free to speak as they like when conducting their official duties.”

The three employees received termination notices on Aug. 21 and were given a five-day period to challenge the action. The Pentagon, however, agreed not to finalize their dismissals before Friday, a step that Judge McFadden’s decision now allows it to take.

Judge McFadden’s ruling rejected only an initial emergency order halting the personnel actions, noting that the plaintiffs had to meet “a heavy burden” of proof to have such an order approved. But Judge McFadden, who was nominated to the court by President Trump early in his first term, appeared skeptical of the lawsuit’s merits.

“Perhaps discovery will strengthen plaintiffs’ case,” Judge McFadden wrote. “But at bottom, on the current record, plaintiffs’ real complaint seems to be that they were victims of a cruel bait-and-switch. They are being fired for giving pre-approved interviews on their paper’s behalf in which they largely toed the company line. Whatever else such a scheme may violate, it does not clearly offend the First Amendment.”

Judge McFadden was also skeptical of the journalists’ argument that they were fired in retaliation for writing about the deteriorating morale on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln.

Judge McFadden wrote that “the U.S.S. Lincoln piece was written by a reporter other than Korte, and plaintiffs do not contend that Slavin or Lederer were directly involved,” adding that “plaintiffs themselves allege that Lederer had already received criticism related to the CBS News interview before publication of the U.S.S. Lincoln story. And the Department’s declarant states that the notices for Slavin and Korte were completed on Aug. 6, also prior to the story.”

In a statement, the three Stars and Stripes employees expressed disappointment in the ruling and noted that the broader case “remains unresolved.”

“We continue to believe that the Pentagon should not be able to fire journalists for speaking out against censorship and defending the editorial independence of Stars and Stripes,” they said in the statement.

item.title: In Major Leak Hunt, Pentagon Gives Polygraph Tests to Joint Staff Members
item.description:
U.S. government investigators have taken the extraordinary step of subjecting roughly 50 members of the U.S. military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists, including about how the Iran war has created a shortage of crucial munitions, according to officials briefed on the move.

The investigators asked military officers and civilian employees on the Joint Staff if they disclosed classified information to members of the press, and about whether they provided information about diminished U.S. munitions stocks.

The polygraph tests were conducted in August after a flurry of news reports detailed diminished stocks of crucial munitions, including of long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors. The show of force appeared aimed at not just ferreting out anyone who may have shared information, but intimidating others who might do so in the future, according to people with knowledge of the effort.

Between 1,500 and 2,000 officers and officials work for the Joint Staff, which coordinates operations, policy and war plans with combatant commanders around the world.

In a statement, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that the department “does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”

“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” he added.

The scope of the investigation is without parallel. Mass polygraph tests have never been administered to the top ranks of the U.S. military in modern history.

“I’ve never seen polygraphs employed this broadly or at this seniority level,” said Rear Adm. Donald J. Guter, a retired top judge advocate general for the Navy from 2000 to 2002. “In my experience, it’s unprecedented.”

The move comes as multiple news organizations have revealed details about how the war with Iran has drained munition stockpiles and reported on concerns inside the administration about the strategic direction of the conflict.

President Trump has pressured administration officials to aggressively hunt for those leaking information. But the president has gone further than merely trying to stop the flow of unauthorized information; he has labeled “treasonous” the media coverage that is critical of the U.S. handling of the war in Iran and the shortages of munitions.

The leaks have intensified an atmosphere of deep distrust and paranoia inside the Pentagon, one that current and former officials say has been fostered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Surrounded by a tight inner circle of loyalists, Mr. Hegseth has pushed out or blocked the promotions of at least 80 generals, admirals and other officials during his tenure. Since early last year, the Pentagon has been conducting a number of leak investigations in response to news coverage about his leadership, even as he faced criticism for sharing sensitive details about strikes in Yemen in a Signal group last year.

Mr. Hegseth has not given a briefing to the Pentagon press corps about the U.S. war in Iran since May 5 and has sought to limit the access of journalists at the Pentagon, a policy that The New York Times has challenged in court.

Last month, the Defense Department fired the publisher and the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news outlet that reports on the U.S. military, a move the journalists said was retribution for their coverage of the worsening conditions on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln.

Mr. Trump has stood by Mr. Hegseth, saying he is doing a “fantastic job,” despite growing concerns about the leadership turmoil inside the Pentagon.

Recently, some Republicans on Capitol Hill have begun publicly voicing criticism of the Pentagon secretary, saying he is mistreating top officials.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina and a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, wrote in a social media post this week, calling on Mr. Trump to replace Mr. Hegseth.

“He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Mr. Tillis said.

Mr. Tillis was among the senators who voted to confirm Mr. Hegseth for the role in early 2025, despite having voiced concerns about his nomination.

item.title: Former Kentucky Governor Is Arrested Amid Child Support Battle
item.description:
Matthew Bevin, a former governor of Kentucky, was arrested on Thursday after resisting court orders in a legal dispute over child support payments, the authorities said.

Mr. Bevin, a Republican who was governor from 2015 until 2019, was picked up while on a movie set after a judge issued an arrest warrant, officials said.

The judge, Angela J. Johnson of Jefferson County Family Court, had ordered Mr. Bevin to turn over documents disclosing his income and assets to finalize child support payments to his son Jonah Bevin.

But Mr. Bevin, 59, has repeatedly failed to file those papers, John Helmers Jr., a lawyer for Jonah Bevin, said on Friday.

“There is profound sadness in that Jonah must watch his father choose jail over fulfilling his obligations to support his son,” Mr. Helmers and a co-counsel for Jonah, Melina Hettiaratchi, said in a news release. “Jonah did not seek this public conflict.”
